# Preparation and Fixation of Saltpeter / for the purpose of making the Red Sulfur fixed.
<note>"Fixed" refers to a substance that has been rendered stable under heat, so it no longer evaporates or burns.</note>

Have a suitable jar made for you, and in it melt two pounds of antimony <note>original: *Antimonium*</note>. And when it has melted, gradually add saltpeter <note>original: *Salniter*</note> to it, one assay-spoonful at a time. Do this until you have added all the saltpeter; then let it flow quite gently. Then pour the entire matter into a large mold <note>original: *Buckel*</note> or vessel; the saltpeter will remain in the upper part, and the antimony will be underneath, and it will become a regulus <term>König: Literally "king," the heavy metallic part of an ore that settles at the bottom of a crucible.</term>. Melt the regulus again with saltpeter, as before, and you will have fixed saltpeter. There should be as much saltpeter as there is regulus. This saltpeter does not burn. Grind it, and set it out to dissolve <note>original: *solvieren*; likely referring to deliquescence, where a salt absorbs moisture from the air to become a liquid oil.</note>, and it will become a yellow oil. With this oil, one fixes the sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*</note> that has been prepared as mentioned above.

Afterward, take one part of the redness of antimony and two parts of the prepared sulfur; grind them together very finely, put them into a glass, and imbibe <note>soak or saturate</note> them with the saltpeter oil, stirring well with a wooden stick so that the material becomes quite moist. Afterward, let the moisture evaporate <note>original: *verriechen*</note> over a gentle heat. And when it is quite dry, grind it again, and imbibe it more with the saltpeter oil. Perform this imbibing, drying, and grinding five times, and you will see whether the sulfur is fixed or not. Test it like this: Take a small sheet of silver, make it red-hot, and place the sulfur upon it. If it still smokes, then imbibe it, dry it, and grind it again—and repeat this with the saltpeter oil until the sulfur flows upon the silver sheet without any smoke. With this fixed sulfur, fix the silver in the following manner.

Take finely filed silver and make small sheets from it; take one mark <term>Marck: A traditional European unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams.</term> of these, and make layer upon layer <note>original: *stratum super stratum*</note> with the sulfur and silver. There should be three loth <term>Loth: A unit of weight, about 1/16th of a pound or 14-15 grams.</term> of sulfur to one mark of silver, well-sealed with lute <note>original: *verlutiert*; sealed with a clay paste to make it airtight</note> in a crucible, and placed in a reverberatory furnace <note>original: *Reverber Ofen*; a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note>; let it reverberate well for eight hours. Afterward, place it in a wind furnace and let it flow well together. Then refine it on a cupel <term>Capellen: A shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</term> or a testing-shard, as you know how to do. Perform this cementing and refining four times. I have done it three times, and in the mark of silver, I found beautiful, stable, and high-grade gold worth 9 gulden.

# A true procedure with talc, to fix the Mercury, and likewise to make the spirits in the nitric acid fixed so that they coagulate together with the Mercury.
<note>"Fixing" a substance means making it resistant to heat so it does not evaporate.</note>

Take one part talc <term>Talck: In alchemy, this often refers to mica or translucent minerals rather than modern cosmetic talc; it was highly prized for its supposed ability to resist fire.</term>—which can be found in the apothecary—the "Star of the Moon" <note>original: *Stellam Lunæ*; likely a specific crystalline form of silver or a mineral</note>, and one part saltpeter. Grind them together, put them into a good crucible or small pot, seal it very well with lute <note>original: *verlutiers*; a clay paste used to make vessels airtight</note>, and place it in a fire, under a salt pan, or a brick kiln. Let it burn well for three days and nights. Or, place it in a wind-furnace <note>a furnace with a strong natural draft</note> and only take care that the seal does not break and the matter does not evaporate <note>original: *außrieche*; literally "smell out"</note>. And when it has stood for the three days, take it out; it should be of a green color, then it is correct.

Then take a parting-water <term>Scheidwasser: Nitric acid, used to "part" or separate silver from gold.</term> made of saltpeter, vitriol, and alum. Once the water is made, take as much of the water as you wish and throw a little of the above-mentioned material into it—it must be ground small—and it will dissolve quickly. Then throw a little more in, and continue doing this until it will no longer dissolve. Then the spirits dissolve and coagulate the water like a jelly. Then for every three *Loth* <note>a weight unit, approximately 15 grams</note> of the water, take one *Loth* of Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>; add the Mercury to it and draw off the water <note>distill it</note>. Do this four or five times, and a beautiful precipitate <note>original: *Præcipitat*</note> will remain. Then you can equalize the Silver <note>original: *Lunam*</note> and the Sulfur so that they flow <note>melt</note> together by the light of a candle. With that same equalized material, imbibe <note>soak</note> the Mercury into the lead and then cupel it <note>original: *abtreib*; a process of refining precious metals by burning off base metals</note>. Thus, from one *Loth* of Mercury precipitate, you will keep one *Quintlein* <note>about 3.75 grams</note> of Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> that is almost golden.

For this, I have taken one part saltpeter, one part talc, and one and a half parts tartar <note>original: *Tartarum*</note>.

### Coagulation of Mercury with Talc.

Take the talc which is called "Star of the Earth" <note>original: *Stella Terræ*; likely a reference to a specific variety of mica or a sparkling mineral</note>, roast it, and wash it three times in Oil of Tartar <term>Oleo Tartari: A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used by alchemists as a powerful alkaline solvent.</term>. Then take one part of this talc and half a part of litharge <term>Glett (Glätte): Lead oxide, often used as a flux in smelting to help metals flow.</term>, ground fine. Mix them together, place the mixture in a crucible, and set it before a bellows. Let it melt thoroughly so that it quickly reaches a liquid state. And when it has flowed, pour it into a casting mold <note>original: *Gießbuckel*</note> and tap upon it; the lead will then settle at the bottom into a "king" <term>König: A regulated button of pure metal found at the bottom of a crucible after the impurities have been separated.</term>, and the talc will lie on top, having turned into dross <note>original: *Schlacken*</note>. Grind this dross. If you add lead to it, you will find the same result a second time.

Afterward, take Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> that has been prepared upon lead, and dissolve it in a common nitric acid <term>Aquafort: *Aqua fortis*, a powerful acid used to dissolve silver and other metals.</term> that is strong. Once the mercury is dissolved, add an equal amount of the prepared lime <note>referring to the calcined talc/dross mentioned previously</note>; in this way, the mercury unites with the talc. Then draw the water off using an alembic <term>Alembicum: A distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term> and take the matter out of the glass, grinding it to a powder.

Next, take two crucibles, let them become hot and glow, and in one crucible melt 4 *loth* <term>Loth: A pre-metric German unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 14.5 grams or half an ounce.</term> of lead. When the lead is flowing well, pour 1 *loth* of the powder from the glass into the other hot crucible, and quickly pour the molten lead over it. Stir it all together with a piece of wood and let it flow together for one hour. Then pour it into a casting mold to form a king. Break this king in half, and cupel <term>treibe ab: The process of refining precious metals by heating them in a shallow cup (cupel) to oxidize and remove base metals like lead.</term> the other half. Thus, one *loth* of mercury yields a *quintlein* <term>Quintlein: A small unit of weight, approximately 3.6 grams.</term> of silver that is nearly golden.

Afterward, make a strong alkaline lye from two parts lime and one part beechwood ashes; pour this three times over fresh lime and ashes, and distill it through a filter. Now, take one part of the cinnabar in a crucible and one part of the salt, and let them melt very well together, so the cinnabar remains "fixed" <note>meaning it has become resistant to evaporation by fire</note> at the bottom. Repeat this melting three times, and the cinnabar is ready.

### To fix copper.

Take one pound of arsenic, one pound of alum, one pound of saltpeter, one pound of talc, one pound of tartar, and then Oil of Tartar <term>Oleum Tartari: A concentrated potassium carbonate solution.</term>. ### To bring gold into silver.

Imbibe the powder with Oil of Alkali three times, and then it is ready.

## The Practice upon Silver in this Work.

Take one part of fine mill-sand <note>fine silica sand</note>—cut it from where there is no lime—one and a half parts glass, and one and a half parts of heavy smithy-sand <note>iron scales or slag from a forge</note> that is as heavy as lead and shaped like a marcasite <term>Marcasit: A mineral (iron pyrite) or a metallic bismuth/antimony formation.</term>. ## To bring Gold into Silver.

Take two parts of salt <note>original: *Salch*, likely a dialect variant of *Salz* or referring to a specific flux salt</note> and one part of antimony <note>original: *Spießglaß*</note>; grind it all small, mix it together, seal it with luting, and place it in a pot. Then, while it is still hot, place it in a kettle of water and let it boil for two good surges. Afterward, pour it through a lye-bag <note>a cloth filter</note>. Take that same filtered lye and strike it again with distilled spirits <note>original: *gebrandtem Wein*, literally "burnt wine"</note> using just a few droplets. This residue, when soaked into the melt, turns gold into silver <note>likely referring to a process of whitening gold or creating a specific alloy</note>. Let the water stand in a gentle heat.

### not for the common sort.
## Albertus Magnus,
->writes thus in the first book of the *Naturalia* <note>original: *Naturalium*; refers to Albertus Magnus's major work on natural philosophy</note>, in the third chapter.<-

In every transformation of the elements, a certain suffering <note>original: *Leiden*; in alchemical philosophy, this refers to a "passion" or a passive state a substance enters before its nature is changed</note> occurs first, so that the powers or virtues of the changed element take on or adopt a form within it from the transformation of the substance. And once they have been mixed into some element, that element will have a material—by which it is an element—possessing the virtue and power of the other element.

And this is the highest ingenuity of the masters of nature. For Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary mythical founder of alchemy</note> teaches, in the Book of Secrets, regarding the most hidden things, with veiled words or through parables. Thus our Stone proceeds with great cunning; it ascends from the earth into heaven, and again down to the earth. 
> Its nurse is the earth, and the wind has carried it in its belly. <note>This is a famous excerpt from the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational text of Western alchemy.</note>

When he took it upon himself to teach the art of <term>Alchemy</term>, he said: It ascends into heaven, where it takes on the property of fire through its cooking and <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>. For the alchemists call <term>calcination</term>—which happens through <term>precipitation</term> and cooking—the making of a <term>material</term> into a powder. This <term>material</term> then descends again from heaven to the earth, as it takes on the virtue and power of the earth through burial <note>Often refers to placing the alchemical vessel in the ground or in warm horse dung to maintain a steady, gentle heat.</note>. When that has occurred, that which was previously killed through the <term>calcination</term> is made living and awakened again through the burial.

But where he says, "The wind has carried it in its belly": here he indicates the governance or purification of the material, <gloss>so that</gloss> it attains the virtues or powers of the air. And for that reason he says, "The wind carries the material in its belly."

The four smells are Good, Stinking, Sharp, and Raw. The two genders are Male and Female. The two heights: the High is the Manifest, but the Deep is the Hidden or Secret, and the Breadth shares in both of these.

Therefore, one should understand all bodies according to these three dimensions. Because of this, a body in its height is earthly; thus it is cold, dry, melancholic, sour, stinking, and female. ## Of the Nature and Property of Azoth.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring a floral or landscape scene.</image-desc>
The child **Azoth** <term>Azot; the "universal medicine" or essential transformative agent, often identified with Mercury</term> is of the lineage of Alum, and is red-colored, yellow, or green on the outside or in the manifest, and on the inside or in the hidden, it is a red-colored silt—the very fattest part of the ore or of the earth. But it is an obstacle, acting harshly on the tongue and making the mouth pucker <note>original: *rumpffen*</note> just like white alum. Therefore it is called by the Sages "Red Alum" or "**Red Roman Oil**" <note>original: *Oleum rubeum Romanum*</note>. It is also called Ⓐ <note>alchemical symbol for Salt or Vitriol</note> and "**Holy Earth**" <note>original: *Tera Sanctum*</note> of the Sages, which is then very necessary for the **Tincture** <term>the concentrated power used to color or transform metals</term> and the coloring of **Sol** <note>original: *Solis*; the Sun or Gold</note>, and to subdue or retain the metals. Concerning this, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century alchemist</note> writes to his son thus: This is the origin of our work in this art, and in the coloring or Tincture of Sol it is greatly exalted, coloring through itself, and increasing with the addition of the Tincture—and it is a light of all lights.

But it is of itself of hard penetration, unless it is added to the oil which is the head of all oils, which colors perfectly and penetrates whatever it bodily colors with it. And there is no other thing that has all salts within it; and it is the bitter salt of which the Sages say much. There is also no other thing that can so perfectly color the "Stone of Vapors"—"a stone, and not a stone"—as this brief Azoth. And it is a Tincture that increases the redness, without which alone the **Elixir** <term>the transformative substance, often the liquid form of the Philosopher's Stone</term> of growing things is colored.

### Of the Philosophical Stone

the elixir is composed of the red thing and from red things.

One reads in the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages</note> that if anything true is found in the art of **Alchemy** <note>original: *Alchemiæ*</note>, it is nothing else than adding the moist to the dry. All the natural masters say this. By "the dry," one understands the perfect, pure **body** <note>the solid, material substance</note> when it has been turned into ash or reduced to a state of ash; and by "the moist," one understands the **spirit** <note>the volatile or liquid principle</note> when it has been cleansed of all impurity.

And truly, this composition consists entirely of **dissolution** <term>Solutio; the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</term> and **coagulation** <term>Coagulatio; the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</term>. Dissolution, according to the opinion of the natural masters, is bringing the body to the nature of the spirit. Coagulation is bringing the spirit to the nature of the body. And thus the body becomes spiritual, and the spirit becomes corporeal. In this way, the words and sayings of the masters are fulfilled, who say: "The fixed shall become volatile, and the volatile shall become fixed." And thus you may obtain the entire mastery by the grace of God.

And God knows that this dissolution may never happen without the **transmutation of the elements**. Therefore, one reads in the *Turba Philosophorum*: "Turn your elements, and you will find the thing you seek." Truly, the turning of the elements is nothing other than transforming one element into the nature of another.

The natural masters say: That in every "enclosed weather" <note>likely referring to the atmosphere or a sealed vessel mimicking celestial conditions</note> in the heavens, four elements are present in essence, though they are not visible. And they say: That no thing may arise or be born without the four elements. Yet, in various ways of "elementing" <note>the process of balancing or arranging the elements</note>, the mixed things dominate in various forms. As in the Stone of the natural masters, who say: Our Stone is composed of a body and a spirit. One clearly sees in the spirit of our Stone that Water and Air have the upper hand over the other elements: yet **Fire** <note>symbol: $\triangle$</note> surpasses the Air. Therefore, the spirit, by its own nature and power, cannot have rest nor endure in the sharpness of the **Fire** <note>symbol: $\triangle$</note>. For the Fire is hot and dry, and the water is cold and moist.

As to how the transformation of the elements may happen, you are perhaps well-informed. You also have a beautiful saying of **Albertus Magnus** <note>a 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath often cited as an alchemical authority</note> at the very beginning of these **quires** <note>original: *Quaternlins*; small gatherings of folded pages</note>, taken from the **third book of the Natural Conflicts** <note>original: *ex tertio libro Naturalium Bellorum*</note>. The natural master says: See that your **putrefaction** <note>original: *Feulung*; the stage of "blackness" where matter decomposes to be reborn</note> is neither too cold nor too warm; perform your work gently and wisely.

One should take the **Stone** <term>The Stone; the "Philosopher’s Stone," the legendary substance sought by alchemists to perfect matter</term>, which is known from the previous chapter, and then handle it with steady practice of the work. ### Of the Philosopher’s Stone

The artists of **Alchemy** <term>Alchemia; the ancient art of transformation, aimed at perfecting both metals and the human spirit</term> say that the essential forms of metals cannot be truly transformed as they are: But it follows thereafter / Unless / a reduction into their first nature occurs.

For the material of all metals, as said before, is found in **Mercury** <term>Quecksilber; quicksilver, viewed by alchemists as the "mother" or the primal fluid matter of all metallic bodies</term>. At first, it is a water, but such water is very closely aligned with nature—indeed, almost natural—and by its hand, Nature itself is assisted by this art. Because of the difficulty of this work, many have been made fools by this art, having spent their youth and their wealth upon it. There are as many error-filled books as there are follies. So many manual labors are performed by these incapable or ignorant workers. Even the strongest man despairs of the art, so that he does not attain the highest deed, or the fruit of the end.

But when I observed all things, and how the kings <note>The author likely refers to "Sovereigns of the Art," the elite masters who claimed to have achieved the Great Work, or perhaps actual royal patrons.</note> performed clever and subtle work yet could seldom reach perfection, I thought this art was nothing. But when I came to myself again and paid attention to the books, **The Secret of Secrets of Aristotle** <note>original: *De Secretis Secretorum Aristotelis*; a famous medieval treatise on statecraft and occult sciences once attributed to Aristotle</note> and **Avicenna** <note>original: *Auicennę*; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy</note>, that is, to the books of hidden and secret things: I found them empty or hollow of natural causes, despite how highly they guard their secrets and recount them in hiding. I avoided those books that argue against the art, and I discovered their errors and changes / just as I also paid attention to the beginnings or origins of natural things. Through this, I found that the work can indeed happen, or is possible. For I have seen mercury penetrate and other metals grow.

Therefore, I ask that no one presume to begin the work based on the things that shall be said here, unless he be very cautious, experienced, and skilled in natural origins, and very well-informed in minerals, **distillation**, **coagulation**, **dissolution** <term>Dissolution; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid, often seen as the first step in the "Great Work"</term> or dissolving, and most of all in the management of the **fire**. Also, he should not be a man who wishes to hurry, but rather one who works leisurely, with reason, and with purity. Therefore, it is a growing metallic or practical Stone, from which is extracted the power or virtue of the white **Azoth** <term>Azot; the "universal solvent" or the essential transformative agent, often symbolized as the beginning and end of the work</term>, of the red clear radiance, so that they add nothing further to it: And it is extracted through separation, purification, and the joining together of the **four elements**.

## A Complete and True Practice; But Search It Out Rightly, Philosophically and Not Fantastically.

After our stone is placed in our vessel and feels the heat of the sun, it immediately dissolves into water and rises entirely upward into the head of the vessel. And it rises upward through its wind, that is, through the smoke. When the natural masters saw this rising, so that the matter rose upward, they spoke and held a counsel as to what they should call this, and they decided that this should be called their **Sublimation** <term>Sublimation: in alchemy, the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and condenses in the upper part of a vessel</term>. After that, when they saw the matter descending, or sinking to the bottom of the vessel and turning into water, they devised in their hearts that they should call the other by way of **Distillation**, and **Descension** <note>the act of moving downward</note> or **Solution** <note>dissolving</note> and **Dissolution**. And when they saw such rising and falling turning into water, they said that this was the perfect Distillation, which then is the third way; and the falling, which then is the fourth.

Likewise, when they saw that the matter became thick and turned into an earth, and this thickening stood at first on top of the water; and as they let it thus slowly thicken, they saw the earth sink and stay at the bottom of the glass under the water. Which earth was blackish-yellow and filthy or stinking; they devised it in their minds that they should call this effect the **Destruction** <note>original: *Zerstörung*; often called putrefaction, where the matter "dies" and turns black before its rebirth</note>, which then is the fifth way.

Also, when they saw even more of this filthy earth staying under the water, changing color through long cooking in our sun and leaving its evil stench, they called this effect **Albation** <note>original Latin: *Albationem*; the process of whitening or washing the matter to reach the silver stage</note> or washing.

Therefore **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemical secrets to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: You should know that the entire mastery is nothing other than a drawing out of the water from the earth and a pouring of this water onto the earth until the earth **putrefies** <note>decomposes</note> or decays. And this earth decays with this water and is purified; which, when it is purified, the whole mastery is completed with help. Therefore the natural master says: Whiten the **Laton** <term>Laton: a term for the impure metallic "body" (often likened to brass) that must be purified into silver or gold</term>, and put away the books; which then is the sixth way.

Furthermore, when they see the earth staying under the water and growing, and the same water decreasing due to moderate cooking, they said: That it is the perfect **Ceratio** <term>Ceratio (Waxing): the process of softening a hard substance until it becomes waxy and easily melted</term> or growth, and thus it would be its right name. As then the natural master has said: The earth is moistened with the natural water and showered or washed, and is dried through moderate cooking of our sun, and the entire matter is turned into earth. Here **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note>, a father of all natural masters, says: Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. And that is the seventh way.

Also, they saw that the whole matter came to the earth and that it reintroduced itself or made a firm substance or essence, and that it does not flow nor rise, but was constrained; when they saw all this, they said it was the perfect **Coagulation** <note>the thickening or solidification of a liquid</note>. Therefore the master says: Dissolve our stone, and thereafter **coagulate** it again into earth, and that with a great...

**Of Nature and Property**

Preservation or observation / as is now indicated: And so you will almost have the entire secret. And that is the eighth way.

Lucas <note>likely a reference to an early alchemical authority or a specific text attributed to a "Lucidarius"</note> says: That our entire mastery is nothing else / but the right **Solution** <term>Solution: the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</term> or the dissolving / and the right **Coagulation** <term>Coagulation: the thickening or solidifying of a liquid into a solid</term>. Of this Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: Dissolve our stone / and thereafter coagulate it / without any further addition or subtraction by hand / and seek nothing more / then you will have the entire mastery / And when they saw even more / That our matter was calcined <term>Calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</term> / and that same thing was the right calcination. That is the ninth way.

If you now / you sons of the Art or doctrine / behave yourselves rightly according to the time / you will easily reach the end / which otherwise cannot happen. He who plants fruit trees / does not hope to gather fruit / except at the time of harvest. Therefore you will have the Art / if you see or read one of these little books / or if you experience the first regimen. The natural masters have said: That the right is not recognized / without the wrong or error / and nothing brings greater pain to the heart / than error in this Art: When one thinks / he has almost the whole world / yet finds nothing in his hands.

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many alchemical works are attributed</note> says: Since in such great age I did not cease for a long time to ponder or experiment / I have spared my soul / so that I would not damn it / by withholding this wisdom or Art. For the understanding of this Art I hold only to be the inspiration of the one God / who has deigned / to reveal it to you, His servant, in the most true and proven way. For He gives us the choice or power of our free will. Yet He gives no one cause / nor any excuse for sin. Truly / if I did not fear the Day of Judgment / I would reveal nothing of this Art. But I have given the faithful and the fortunate their justice / as the Lord has given to me.

Geber: He who does not know the natural beginnings and origins within himself / is very far from the Art of the philosophers / For he has no ground / upon which he sets or builds his designs or opinions. But if he knows the natural origin of himself / and all causes are not unknown to him / then he will soon arrive at the beginnings of the Art. And although a man knows or recognizes the matter / he still lacks many things for the completion.

O you bitter watery form or shape / you who dissolve the elements. O you greatest nature / who overcomes the mediocre nature / who comes with the light / and is born of the light / and who has given birth to the mists / who is a mother of all things. And thus is the end.

Praise and honor be to God the Father / and His only begotten Son / and the Comforter the Holy Spirit / the triune eternal Lord and God / who reigns through and through without end / from world to world / Amen.

# Of the Philosophical Stone.

I, who have written these things, have seen all these things until now. I pray to God that He may grant me grace to also see the end one day.

->God will give. <note>original: "DEVS dabit"</note> Note well, my Son. <note>original: "Nota bene, mi Fili"</note><-

Son, now I will lead you into the **Garden of Delight** and all voluptuousness, and into its **Bath**, in which its power is generated or multiplied without end. And as often as you shall carry it upon this Stone, it is perfect and most pure in the fire, without any blemish. Then you shall rub it almost to a subtle powder upon a stone in our most noble, most subtle **Vinegar** <term>Vinegar: in alchemy, this usually refers to a potent acidic solvent or "Acetum Philosophorum," not common table vinegar</term>; dissolve it, and immediately it will be dissolved into the most beautiful **Water of the Philosophers**. And when our Stone is entirely dissolved, as I have said, then distill it through our distillation and coagulate it with tempered heat; and it consists in the best way, according to the coagulation, by the manner as stated. And you, Son, shall know that in the 4th **Solution** <term>Solution: the process of turning a solid into a liquid</term>, one part **tinges** <term>Tinge: to transform or dye the nature of a base metal into a noble one</term> 100 parts of ☿ <note>Mercury</note>, or of any **Body** <term>Body: a term for a solid metal</term>, into true Silver or Gold, according to how the Stone is prepared. And that is our salvation and the **Secret of all Secrets**.

->T H E   E N D.<-

# OIL OF ANTIMONY:
## The Fixation, its Quintessence.
### Caspar Oberlein.

Take one pound of ♁ <note>Antimony</note>, one pound of **Salt of Tartar** <term>Salt of Tartar: Potassium carbonate, often used as a flux</term>, rub it all small together, and put it into a crucible; let it flow in a wind-furnace for half an hour. Then pour it onto a stone and rub it very small again. Put the same into a glass and pour good, rectified **Aqua vitæ** <term>Aqua vitæ: "Water of Life," a term for concentrated distilled alcohol</term> or brandy upon it; place it in gentle heat for eight days, and it will become golden yellow. Then pour that off into a clean glass, well-stoppered, and then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon it. Place it in the heat for eight days, or as long as it takes until it colors itself again as before, and it will then also become yellow. Pour that then with the other yellow ▽ <note>Water/Liquid</note>, and then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon it again. Continue this pouring on and drawing off as long and as often until it extracts no more yellowness. Then distill the yellow Aqua vitæ off via a **Water Bath** <note>original: "per Baln." (per balneum)</note>, so that a thick **Oil** remains. And the Aqua vitæ is always good to draw out more in this work. When you have drawn off the yellow Aqua vitæ down to the **Oil** <note>original: "Oleum"</note>, and when one coagulates that same Oil again into a powder or mass, that same thing may then truly be the **Quintessence**, as I am certainly assured.

Afterward, take twice as much **brick-dust** as there is of the Oil, and mix it well together, and put it into a small flask, and lay it on its side in the furnace with a receiver before it; and distill it like a water, at first with gentle fire and at last very strong; thus the Oil will pass over or rise up entirely red, and then it is prepared.

Afterward, take three parts of **living** ☿ <note>Mercury</note> and one part of ☉ <note>Gold</note>, amalgamate them together, and then pour the Oil upon it, so that it stands a thumb's breadth above it. And then place it in ashes for four or five days in gentle heat; thus the **Amalgam** will become entirely black, and hard-coagulated, and **fixed** <term>Fixed: a substance that is no longer volatile and can withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating</term>. Then pour the Oil off and keep it, for it is always good as long as it lasts. Then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon the coagulated mass of ☉ <note>Gold</note> and ☿ <note>Mercury</note>, and wash the Oil of ☉ <note>Gold</note> clean from it; it dissolves into the Aqua vitæ. Then distill the Aqua vitæ down through an **Alembic** in a Water Bath until the Oil remains. Put that Oil then with the first Oil; it is then always as good as the first. Reduce the coagulated mass with **Borax** <note>original: "Purras"</note>; thus there remains three parts of Gold at twenty-four degrees <note>referring to 24-karat purity</note>.

<page-num>580</page-num>
<header>Of the Oil of Antimony. <note>original Latin: "De Oleo Antimonij"</note></header>

### How to extract the Quintessence from Antimony ore.

Take Antimony ore, pound it or rub it into a fine powder until it becomes very subtle. After that, take the very best distilled wine vinegar you can find and pour it into a glass flask <note>specifically a "Kolbenglaß" or retort</note>, and pour the powder into it so that the vinegar stands about two fingers' width above it. Stir it well together, then let it stand in gentle heat for 8 days, or until the vinegar turns red. Pour off that red-colored liquid and keep it clean. Pour more vinegar onto the powder as before, and let it stand as before. Take the redness from it again, along with the vinegar, as before. Continue this pouring off and extraction until the vinegar no longer turns red.

Afterward, put the colored material into a flask and distill it very gently through an alembic <note>a "per Alembicum" distillation apparatus used for purifying liquids</note>. First, a white phlegm <term>Phlegm: in alchemy, this refers to the tasteless, watery byproduct of distillation</term> or water will come over. Then, it will come over in red drops. At that point, take away the receiver and put another one in its place. Then collect the redness separately; that is the true Quintessence of Antimony. Use it then as you know how. It has a sweet taste like honey.

Also, the vinegar along with the extracted Antimony must first stand for 40 days in dung for putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: the process of allowing a substance to rot or ferment in a warm environment, often simulated by burying the flask in a warm dung heap</term>, and decay in the glass, well-sealed; only then should it be worked as indicated above. The Oil of Antimony is as excellent a medicine for wounds as any to be found on earth. The *Pleyl* <note>likely "Bleiglanz" or galena, a lead ore often associated with antimony</note> is almost equal to it; you will find that in another booklet.

### To extract the Sulfur from Antimony.

Take two ounces <note>original: "Loth"</note> of Saltpeter, one pound of Vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate</note>, and eight ounces of Alum. From these, a water is distilled as is customary, and the spirits are driven out strongly. Pour this *Aqua Fortis* <term>Aqua Fortis: "Strong Water," or nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</term> onto pounded ♁ <note>Antimony</note> in a "Benedict flask" so that it covers it slightly. Let it stand for one day, and the Antimony will draw the *Aqua Fortis* entirely into itself. Then pour more *Aqua Fortis* over it so that it is well covered, by about two or three fingers' width. Afterward, distill the *Aqua Fortis* back off through the alembic with very gentle heat and slowly. Thus the ♁ <note>Antimony</note> rises over with the *Aqua Fortis* through the alembic, and the Sulfur remains lying at the bottom, white and coarse. It becomes so hard that it cannot be removed, and the glass must be broken. And if the Sulfur still has moisture in it, it must be dried on a lime kiln. Afterward, use the Sulfur as you know how. Also, one might try the distilled water for something; it may without doubt be useful for something.

### A work of Antimony by "part for part." <note>original Latin: "pars cum parte," a method of alloying or refining</note>

Take Tartar <note>potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking</note>, Saltpeter, and common salt in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note>; rub it all fine together, put it in a new, unglazed pot, and luten <note>seal with clay</note> a piece of brick on top of it. Place it in a charcoal fire and let it calcine <term>Calcine: to roast or heat a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to powder</term> well, for about a good hour, in good heat. Then when it has cooled, you will find the Tartar calcined white. Then pound that material into a fine powder and dissolve it in hot water. Throw away the dregs <note>original: "Feces"</note>, then filter the dissolved liquid and boil it down into salt.

Afterward, take one pound of Antimony, rub it fine, and mix half a pound of the salt described above into it. Mix it well together, then let it melt thoroughly in a crucible. Afterward, pour it into a casting basin; keep that King <term>King: also called a "Regulus," the button of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible after melting</term>. Pound the slag fine, but add half as much salt to it, mixing it well together, and let it melt as before. Pour it to the King as before; keep the Kings together. Continue this work as long as it produces a King.

Afterward, pound all the Kings together into a fine powder. Take fine, small-grained ☾ <note>Silver</note> equal in weight to the powder of ♁ <note>Antimony</note>. Mix it well together and let it melt together. Pour it into a casting basin, and the ☾ <note>Silver</note> will settle as a King. Take that King out and let the Antimony "smoke away" <note>evaporate through heat</note> from it; then the ☾ <note>Silver</note> will be heavier than before. Afterward, take another pound of fresh Antimony and work it into a King as before. Work all those Kings again with this ☾ <note>Silver</note>, as above <note>original: "ut supra"</note>. And do the same a third time with a pound of fresh ♁ <note>Antimony</note>, as before.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for working with Antimony, specifically detailing the "cementing" and "grading" of metals. It follows the previous page's discussion on extracting the quintessence and transitions into metallurgical applications.</meta>

<page-num>581</page-num>
<header>Of the Oil of Antimony. <note>original Latin: "De Oleo Antimonij"</note></header>

When the Silver <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna)</note> has smoked off for the third time on the shard in the flux, then take that same Silver and place it on another shard. Add three times as much Lead as there is Silver, and drive the Antimony <term>Antimony: a semi-metal used in alchemy to "purify" gold and silver, as it reacts with impurities</term> entirely away from it. Afterward, drive it on the cupel <note>a "Test" or cupel is a shallow, porous dish used in assaying</note> until the "Blick" <term>Blick: the sudden "flash" or brightening seen when a precious metal becomes pure during cupellation</term>. After that, take as much Gold <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol)</note> by weight as there is Silver; let them flow together well in a crucible. Then pour it into an ingot <note>original: "Zain"</note> and laminate it <note>hammer it into thin sheets</note>, and cut small plates from it. Wet them in urine and stratify them <term>Stratify: to layer substances, usually for "cementation" where a metal is purified by being heated while packed in a reactive powder</term> with verdigris <note>a green pigment/acetate formed on copper</note>, not in thick layers <note>original Latin: "stratum super stratum"</note>, and seal it up with luting clay. Cement it in sand for two days and nights. Then let all the materials flow together well with Alkali Salt in a crucible; in this way, the Silver has been graded <note>refined or "exalted" in quality</note> with the Gold to 24 degrees <note>referring to the highest purity, similar to 24-karat</note>.

The slag that remains, let it flow again, so that the remaining Silver settles into a **King** <term>King: also called a "regulus," this is the button of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term>; in this way, you recover all the Silver again.

### A profitable way to bring Gold into a Silver through Antimony, namely one Loth <note>about 1/2 ounce</note> of Gold into one Mark <note>about 8 ounces</note> of Silver at 24 degrees.

You should first purge the Silver <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna)</note> in this way. Take three pounds of rock salt, crush it small, and then rub one pound of unslaked lime into it. Then take a melting crucible, coat the inside with chalk, and then lay in it one Mark of fine Silver, or however much you wish. According to its amount, and for every Mark of Silver, add eight *Loth* of the powder, as described above <note>original Latin: "ut supra"</note>. Seal it with a shard, place it in a wind-furnace <term>Wind-furnace: a blast furnace that uses a strong draft of air to reach the high temperatures needed for melting metals</term>, and let the fire start gently for about an hour. Afterward, give it a strong fire for three hours so that it flows well, until the salt is entirely consumed. After the four hours, lift it out; when it has cooled, you will find the Silver without any loss. Perform this work 4 times, then drive the Silver off in Lead; thus it is purged.

Furthermore, there are many better purifications than this for Silver. Afterward, take eight *Loth* of Antimony <note>original symbol: ♁</note> that has been purged, one and a half *Loth* of Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> filings, one *Loth* of Lead, and one and a half *Quint* <note>a small weight, roughly 1/4 of a Loth</note> of iron filings. Let it all flow together for one hour. Then take it out. When it cools, you will find a beautiful **King**. Then grind one *Loth* of the King and one *Loth* of Silver. Put it in a mortar, or throw a glowing coal into it; stir it well together and let it burn out. Afterward, grind it all small into a powder. With this powder, make layers <note>original Latin: "stratum super stratum"</note> in a cementing shard, the thickness of a knife's back, and use the aforementioned Silver that has been purged. Cover it with a shard on top, and cement it thus for eight hours; the plates will become quite brittle. Afterward, take all the material together as it was in the cement, put it in a crucible, cover it with Venetian glass, and place a shard over it. Let it flow in a wind-furnace for at least one hour. Drive the King for a while on the cupel so that the Antimony smokes away. Then drive it on the cupel to the "Blick." Separate that, and the "lime" <note>calx/powder</note> of the Gold will fall to the bottom; use it as is proper, and the Silver is then at twenty-four degrees.

### To prepare the Antimony for the aforementioned work.

Take one pound of Antimony <note>original symbol: ♁</note>, put it in a crucible, and then pour it into a vessel that has been smeared with a rind <note>animal fat or grease</note>; in this way, its "wildness" <note>volatility or unruly chemical nature</note> is taken from it. Afterward, take the cast Antimony, put it back in a crucible, and add two *Loth* of saltpeter, two *Loth* of **Caput Mortuum** <term>Caput Mortuum: Latin for "dead head," the useless residue left after a chemical distillation—in this case, from making aqua fortis (nitric acid)</term>, two *Loth* of red tartar, and 2 *Loth* of sulfur. Crush everything together and put the powder onto the flowing Antimony. Let it flow well for about a quarter of an hour. Pour it together into a vessel smeared with rind, as before. Thus the Antimony is prepared and black, ready to be used for this work. It also serves goldsmiths for casting Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note>, for it does not "rob" <note>consume or diminish the metal</note as much as raw antimony. Michael Blaman also makes his prepared Antimony in this way, except he takes two *Loth* of Lead and one *Loth* of Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> and no tartar. With that, he grades low-quality Gold and casts through it. I saw this myself in Kutná Hora <note>original: "Küttenberg," a famous silver mining town in Bohemia</note>.

<page-num>182</page-num>
<header>Of the Oil of Antimony. <note>original Latin: "De Oleo Antimonij"</note></header>

### To extract the Quintessence from Antimony, or the Ore.

Take Antimony, as much as you wish, grind it to the smallest size, put it into a glass, and pour very sharp lye upon it, which is made from unslaked lime and willow ash <note>original: "Weidaschen"</note>. Boil the Antimony in it, so the lye becomes red, like blood. Then pour off the lye into a glass, and add another batch of lye, and boil as before until it turns red. Pour it off again, as before. Do this as long as necessary until the lye no longer turns red. Put all the red lye together into a glass, seal it well, and place it in horse manure <term>Horse manure: used by early chemists to provide a gentle, constant heat for fermentation or "digestion"</term> for forty days. Then distill it with a gentle fire; first, pure water comes out. Then red drops come out like blood; collect these separately. With this, you may sublimate Mercury red, and also grade and fixate <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat without evaporating</term> with it. Also, a tincture may be made from it, as I myself know.

### To make the Tartar red for the Antimony.

<margin>Preparation of vinegar for extracting the redness of Mercury. <note>original Latin: "aceti præparatio pro Mercurij rubedine extrahenda"</note></margin>
Likewise, take two quarters of very sharp, distilled vinegar <note>original: "Acetum acerrimum, distillatum"</note>, and one pound of calcined tartar <note>original: "Tartarum calcinatum"</note>. Put the vinegar into a glass flask, and a receiver <term>Receiver: a vessel (Fürlag) used to catch the condensed vapors during distillation</term> before it. Into that [the receiver], put half a pound of calcined tartar, and distill the vinegar over. Then take the receiver away, and pour the vinegar into a flask, and set it in sand. Distill it through an Alembic <term>Alembic: a type of still-head used for distilling liquids</term> into another receiver with the tartar <note>original Latin: "cum Tartaro"</note>. Perform this exchange seven times. Afterward, put all the tartar together into a flask and distill the vinegar from it. At last, give it a good fire, as if you were making Aqua Fortis <term>Aqua Fortis: literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term>; thus the vinegar is prepared.

### Oil of Antimony.

Likewise, take one pound of vinegar and one pound of Antimony, ground very small. Pour the vinegar onto the Antimony in a glass and let it stand in gentle warmth for three days. Thus the vinegar becomes red. Pour this off very carefully so that nothing cloudy goes with it, and pour another batch of vinegar onto it. Let it stand for seven days until the vinegar turns red. Do this until no more redness comes from it. Then distill the vinegar from it through an Alembic, and you will find the Oil of Antimony at the bottom <note>original Latin: "in Fundo"</note>.

### To make Oil of Antimony, and a fixation therewith, to bring four Loth of Gold into one Mark of Silver. <note>A "Loth" was a unit of weight roughly equal to 15 grams; a "Mark" was roughly 230 grams.</note>

Likewise, take black calcined tartar <note>original: "Weinstein"</note>, half a pound, and eight Loth [of Antimony]. Rub it all together, then let it flow in a crucible; cover it with a lid. When it has flowed well, pour it into a sharp vinegar, which should be warm. Let it stand until it becomes clear. Then pour off the vinegar, and you will find the Antimony <note>original: "Spießglaß"</note> lying red on the bottom, like clotted blood; make this into a pure dry powder.

Afterward, take Oil of Tartar <note>original: "Oleum Tartari"</note>, as much as you wish, and dissolve Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to help dissolve metals and minerals</term> in it, as much as can be dissolved. Soak the red Antimony with it, and dry it again. Then grind it, and soak <term>Imbibition: the process of repeatedly soaking a dry powder with liquid and drying it to "feed" the substance</term> it again, as before, and let it become dry. Do this four times. Afterward, place it in a damp cellar, and a red oil will form from it. This is then called Oil of Antimony. And whatever has not dissolved, let it become dry, and grind it small, and soak it again three or four times, as before. Then place it in the cellar, and it will dissolve entirely.

Likewise, make the **second Oil** thus: Take four Loth <term>Loth: a historical unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams or half an ounce</term> of Vitriol <term>Vitriol: a sulfate mineral often used for its acidic properties</term>, dissolve it in urine, and boil it in an unglazed pot <note>original: "unverglasten Hafen"</note> until it is reduced by more than half. Add to it four Loth of Alum <note>symbol: 🜔</note>, three Loth of Saltpeter <note>original: "Saliter"</note>, and four Loth of Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note>, all finely ground. Boil it all until it is dry, turn it into a powder, and place it in a cellar to dissolve <note>The moisture in a damp cellar would cause the salts to deliquesce into a liquid</note>; thus you have the second oil.

Likewise, afterward take these two oils in equal weight or volume. Rub filed Copper <note>symbol: ♀</note> well with them on a hard grinding stone so that it becomes entirely small and subtle. Then put it into a flask <note>original: "Kolbenglaß"</note> and set it to digest for seven days. Pour the oil over it so that it rises just a little above it. And when it has distilled over, pour the distilled water back onto it. Do this seven times. Afterward, put it in a luted <term>Luting: sealing a vessel with clay or paste to make it airtight</term> crucible and let it cement in a low fire for 16 hours; afterward, let it melt in a wind furnace for four hours. Then refine it <note>original: "treibs ab", referring to cupellation</note> in lead and separate it; thus you will find in one Loth of Silver a Quintlin <note>A small weight, 1/4 of a Loth</note> of Gold at 24 degrees <note>referring to high-purity, 24-karat gold</note>.

->**To make Silver from Antimony.**<-

Take <note>original Latin: "Recipe"</note> one pound of Antimony, four Loth of Lead <note>symbol: ♄</note>, and one Loth of Copper <note>symbol: ♀</note>. Let it all melt together in a crucible. Pour it into an ingot mold <note>original: "Gießbuckel"</note>. You should refine this "King" <term>Regulus (King): the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</term> a little on a cupel <note>original: "Treibscherben"</note>, and afterward on the refining test; then you will have the Silver <note>symbol: ☾</note>.

->**To refine Antimony for Gold.**<-

Take two Loth of Sulfur and two Loth of Saltpeter. Grind these two well together. Then place Antimony <note>original: "Spießglaß"</note> in a crucible and let it melt well. Then throw a little of the powder (as described above) into it; cover it with a flask. Then throw a little more into it. Then pour the Antimony into an ingot mold, and it will have a "King" <note>regulus</note>; use it as is proper.

->**To refine Antimony for Silver.**<-

Take one pound of Antimony and two pounds of burnt Tartar <term>Tartar: potassium bitartrate, often obtained from wine barrels and used as a flux</term>. Put these pieces together in a mortar; afterward, put them in a crucible, seal it at the top, and let it melt well. Refine the "King" as is proper.

->**To test the Antimony, to see if it is good for extracting the redness.**<-

Take the Antimony and stroke it upon yellow paper that has been smoothed with a tooth <note>Using a tooth for burnishing paper was a common way to create a perfectly smooth surface for testing mineral streaks</note>. If it leaves a red streak, it is good; but if it leaves a black streak, it is not good. So take the Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note> with the red streaks, grind it small, and mix it with good lime <note>original: "Kalch"</note>. Let there be much more lime than Antimony. Add some clean water to it, let it boil well, then let it settle until clear, and strain it into a glass; then it will be beautifully pure. Then pour distilled wine vinegar into it, and it will turn as if you had poured blood into it. Let it settle, then carefully draw off or drain the liquid. Thus you have a beautiful red powder, which is the **Quintessence of Antimony**.

These pieces should all

...let them all flow together. When it has flowed for half an hour, let it cool so that it settles into a **Regulus** <term>Regulus: the heavy, metallic portion of an ore that sinks to the bottom of a crucible; in German alchemy, this was called the "König" or King</term>; then strike off the Regulus. Take one Loth <term>Loth: a unit of weight, approximately 15–16 grams</term> of the ground Regulus and add it to two Loth of **Silver** <note>symbol: Luna</note>. Let it flow for two hours, then refine it in **Lead** <note>original: "abgetrieben im Pley," referring to cupellation, a refining process where lead is oxidized to separate it from precious metals</note>. This Silver receives all degrees of improvement in the addition, as follows:

### Gradation. <note>Gradation: a process intended to increase the purity, color, or weight of a precious metal</note>

Take Verdigris <note>original Latin: "viridi Aeris"</note>, **Oil of Salt** <note>symbol: 🜖</note>, **Oil of Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note>, and **Oil or Powder of Mercury** <note>symbol: ☿</note>, of each an equal part <note>original Latin: "ana"</note>. If you can obtain **Oil of Iron** <note>original: "Oleum Martis"</note>, take one part of that as well. Put it all together, and when it is coagulated, dissolve it again in a cellar <note>The humidity of a cellar causes certain salts to absorb moisture and turn into liquid</note> or in a "Graduation Water" <note>original: "Aqua, das zum gradieren gemacht ist"</note>. And the more often you do this, the further it tinges <note>The "tinge" refers to the alchemical power to transform the color and nature of a base metal into gold</note>. If a third or fourth part of this powder is thrown into the molten metal, it brings forth **Gold** <note>symbol: ☉</note>.

### To extract the Redness of Antimony, which is used for gradation and fixation. <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term>

Take as much **Tartar** <term>Tartar: "Weinstein," the potassium bitartrate crusts found in wine barrels</term> as you wish in a pot, luted <term>Luted: sealed with an airtight clay or paste</term> at the top; place it in a furnace and let it burn until it no longer smokes; then it is sufficiently turned to black. Pour warm water over it repeatedly until it is no longer "sharp" <note>The sharpness indicates the presence of alkaline salts; the water extracts these to make a lye</note>. Then boil this same lye in a cauldron or glazed pot until it becomes a salt; keep that. Take as much **Antimony** as you wish in a crucible, let it flow gently, and throw the above-described salt into it, finely crushed, for as long and as much as it takes until the **Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note> becomes red. Use this for cementing or grading.

Hammer this Antimony into pieces and pour a good **vinegar** over it; the vinegar will pull the redness entirely out until no more red remains. This is also used for grading. But if you strain off the vinegar, as before, that is the most noble way: when fixed Silver, beaten into thin sheets, is stratified <note>placed in alternating layers</note> beneath it, sealed in a glass or pot with a bit of dough, and held in the fire for a day and a night—first with a gentle heat, then a stronger fire. This **Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note> prepared in this way is good for **Cinnabar** <term>Cinnabar: a bright red mineral, mercury sulfide, often used as a source of mercury or as a pigment</term> in which you wish to fix Silver.

### A small Tincture.

Take **Oil of Mercury** <note>symbol: ☿</note>; dissolve in it **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original symbol: *</note> that has been made red through **Iron** <note>symbol: ♂</note>. Then take **Oil of Vitriol**, and dissolve **Alum** <note>symbol: 🜔</note> in it. Then take both Oils together and let a fourth part evaporate. Afterward, dissolve **Corrosive Sublimate** <note>original Latin: "Mercurium sublimatum"</note> in the oil, for it will dissolve like water. Afterward, take one part of **calcined Gold** <note>symbol: ☉ calcinatum; gold reduced to a fine powder through heat</note>, and moisten it with three parts of the oil, as above <note>original Latin: "ut suprà"</note>. Then place it in warm dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing steady, gentle heat over weeks or months</note>; from this, a very red water will form. Coagulate this with a strong fire, and place it back in the dung. When it has become water again, coagulate it once more. Do this ten times, and it will become a golden water or oil. Then take one part of this oil or water, throw it upon a hundred parts of **raw Mercury** <note>original Latin: "Mercurij crudi"</note>, and it will become good Gold.

# Regarding the Fifth and Final Part
## Preface to the Reader.

Nature, favorable and dear reader, gives us a fine parable, example, and lesson through the bees <note>The author uses the archaic German word "Immen" for bees, a common symbol in early modern literature for industriousness and discernment.</note>, who suck the honey out of all sorts of herbs and flowers—both the poisonous and the non-poisonous—and leave the poison behind. In the same way, we should pick out, draw, and separate the honey alone—that is, the good and useful—from everything we have before us or deal with, and set aside the evil and the worthless. To this, the holy Apostle Paul also points and teaches us through the supernatural light kindled in him in the third heaven, where he says: *Test all things and hold fast only to that which is good.* <note>original Latin: "Omnia probate & solum bonum tenete." (1 Thessalonians 5:21)</note> For we have become subject to good and evil through the Fall of Adam and Eve in original sin, and fire and water are laid before us, with free will given to us to reach for whichever we desire.

For this reason, Nature mixes everything good and evil together for us; she hides nothing by separating or setting it apart. However, she has simultaneously incorporated into us—just as she gave the bees and spiders the power and virtue to draw to themselves, the one the poison and the other the good honey, by an attractive and nourishing power <note>original Latin: "attractiva nutritiva virtute"</note>—perfect understanding, knowledge, and discernment <term>discernment|the ability to judge well or distinguish between things</term> to recognize good and evil, poured into our souls from God's merciful gifts. Thus, we can offer no excuse that we did not know how to distinguish between the good and the evil.

Nature has commanded such innate knowledge and discretion <note>The original term "Discretion" here refers to the power of distinguishing or separating.</note> to us not only in things that fall under reason or the senses <note>original Latin: "rebus quæ sub rationem sive sensus cadunt"</note>, which pertain to reason alone, but she has also left and taught us a certain art in material things, namely Alchemy. Through this art—just as the stomach separates the nourishment from the waste <note>original Latin: "Nutrimentum" and "Excrementum"</note>, or as the vintner <note>original: "Trotner," referring to one who treads or presses grapes.</note> separates the juice and the husks from grapes through the

<summary>This preface introduces the final volume of the alchemical collection by arguing that humans have a divinely given duty to separate the "good" from the "evil" in both spiritual and physical matters, framing alchemy as the tool for this separation in the material world.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, alchemy, Apostle Paul, free will, discernment, separation of substances, bees and spiders, Adam and Eve, philosophy of science</keywords>

...to proceed / in all material things / being able to distinguish and separate the good and the evil from one another.

This art of Alchemy, however—after the tyrannical Emperor Diocletian <note>Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD) reportedly ordered the burning of Egyptian books on alchemy around 297 AD to prevent the production of gold from funding rebellions.</note> had all chemical books burned—was thereafter never again explicitly described. Instead, those who practiced the Philosophical Art sought out the strangest and most unusual names, words, and figures. With these, they hid the secrets of nature <note>original Latin: "Arcana Naturæ"</note> behind strange, wonderful images and under the veil and cover of obscurity. This is apparent in poetic fables and poems, especially in the *History of Fortunatus* <note>A popular European folk tale about a man who receives a bottomless purse and a wishing hat; here, the author views it as an alchemical allegory.</note> and Ovid's *Metamorphoses* <note>A Roman narrative poem describing the history of the world through transformations; alchemists often viewed these myths as metaphors for chemical change.</note>, which is a pure hieroglyphic description <note>In this period, "hieroglyphic" referred to symbolic or allegorical representation rather than specifically Egyptian writing.</note> of the changing of forms. In these, the learned and the commentators <term>Expositores|Scholars who interpret or explain the hidden meanings of difficult texts</term> clearly understand what sweet juice lies hidden beneath the outer bark of the fables. Because of this, however, this art has not only gradually fallen into oblivion through the "injury of time" <note>original Latin: "temporis iniuria"</note>, but has also become more an object of suspicion than esteem among the good-hearted. Among the envious, it has grown more into a thing of mockery than wonder, and thus Nature has fallen into darkness.

Now, to offer assistance to oppressed Nature and to bring her art—which has for a long time now lain hidden and despised "under the bench," not without significant loss and damage to the common good (as can be seen from the preface to the first part of this work)—back into the sunshine and the light of day, I have undertaken a work that is difficult for me personally, given the many hostile eyes watching. This work involves bringing the writings of the ancient philosophers and spagyrists <term>Spagirorum|Alchemists who followed the Paracelsian tradition of "spagyria," the art of separating and then recombining substances to create potent medicines</term>, as well as various treatises <note>original German: "Tractaͤtlin," or "little treatises."</note> collected from all sorts of authors, into the light through public printing. I will, however, gladly bear such a burden with patience and pay little heed to the ignorance and ill-will of enemies, so long as I am comforted by this: that I am doing a favor to the wise and impartial, and that my spirit and intention [is for the] common...

So I now require of the favorable reader’s spirit / not the nature and character of spiders / but of bees (who do not despise any little flower / no matter how small / how poor / how misshapen or poisonous it may be / but take it for themselves / and extract only the good and the honey / leaving the poison for the spiders) who know how to separate and set apart the righteous and good from the evil / the useful from the harmful / the true from the false / and for their own benefit / to pick it out like the nut from the shell / and to cast away the rest which is of no use / for in the same way / as the Art itself is an art of separating and dividing *pari & impari* <note>original Latin: "the equal and the unequal," referring here to the balanced and unbalanced elements of a substance</note> / the evil and the good / the honey from the poison / the wheat from the chaff : So must also in the description of this Art by various authors and conflicting teachings / a separation of the true from the false / and that which was added solely to obscure as useless / be maintained and established / the reason is / that the philosophers mixed everything / truth and lies / proven and unproven / among each other / not only disorderly / and unintelligibly / but wrote the *Contrarium* <note>original Latin: "the contrary"</note> and the reverse / and often on a single page two types of conflicting opinions on one thing / so that one cannot find a way out or conclude / whether they began or ceased to write halfway or entirely / wrongly or rightly. # Preface to the Reader.

...remained and were reserved for the true *Scayolis* <note>original: "Scayolis"; likely referring to the "Scaioli," a term used in some hermetic traditions for those possessed of internal light or spiritual adepts</note> and *Sons of the Art* <note>original Latin: "Filijs artis"</note> alone in secret and in unforgotten *memory* <note>original: "memori"</note> *under unrefined wisdom* <note>original Latin: "sub rudi minerua," an idiom meaning plain, unadorned, or natural knowledge</note>; *Everything should be open to the worthy, but hidden from the profane* <note>original Latin: "Palam omnia dignis, clam verö prophanis essent"</note>. Accordingly, he who wishes to create something fruitful in Alchemy would know well how to maintain a *selection* <note>original Latin: "delectum"</note> and use these books and writings of old and new authors in no other way than a sensible *Architect* <note>original Latin: "Architectus"</note>, who reserves and keeps for himself all kinds of forms and designs of buildings as a pattern, so that these serve him only as a *Memorial* <note>a reminder or record</note>, an example, and to some extent an instruction. Or rather, like a hand <note>a signpost or finger-post</note> on the road, which may lead one just as easily the wrong way as the right, if he is not well-informed of the decision and the roads. Therefore, he must or shall use the books with prudence and understanding in his work and *investigation* <note>original Latin: "Inquisition"</note> of Nature alone, and no further than as a dead letter or a signpost; for this art is so high, magnificent, and great, that in it the whole nature of all things in the entire world is seen, as in a clean, beautiful mirror; and for that reason, it is not for sale at the market, nor to be learned from dead letters, but Nature herself must be sought out in her inner chambers and secrets, and viewed with one's own eyes, since art is and should be a follower of Nature; for no art is valid where Nature is not already present.

But the Art is a *Helper of Nature* <term>Helper of Nature: the alchemical principle that human skill (Art) can accelerate or perfect natural processes that Nature alone cannot complete</term>; she is improved through Art, beyond her natural movement which she had in her first form, and it openly reveals the subtle nature that is enclosed in every thing. For where Nature stops working, there Art first begins, and *perfects* <note>original: "perficiert"</note> Nature, as is clearly seen in almost all things. For *example* <note>original: "Exempel"</note>, we see how Nature brings forth the plants and dear fruits of the earth, and when she has brought them forth, Nature then stops, and Art comes, a helper of Nature, bringing the miller and baker; the miller grinds the grain into flour, from which the baker afterwards makes the dear and holy bread. *Likewise* <note>original Latin: "Item"</note>, as is also to be seen in the mines: there Nature brings forth the ore, but Art takes that same ore and makes from it Gold, Silver, and all kinds of metals which it contains, which Nature would bring forth so slowly if Art did not come to her aid through man. Furthermore, Nature gives birth to wood from the earth, but Art, through fire, makes ash from the wood, and from the ash, a glass—and such *examples* <note>original: "Exempel"</note> there is no need to recount at length. Now, if in the grain, ore, and wood, or ash, this first *Matter* <note>original Latin: "Matery"</note> of the bread, the metals, and the glass were not hidden, then Art would be in no way able to make and bring out what reveals itself, if the...

# Preface to the Reader.

nature was within it. By this it now clearly appears that Nature certainly has within herself what she needs, yet she is not perfected or brought to completion unless she is then moved by her subtle, pleasant, and non-opposing art and <term>operation</term> <note>original: "Operation"; refers to the specific alchemical procedures or manual work</note>; and it is thus sufficiently proven that Art is a helper of Nature.

Since the artist is thus a co-worker and helper of Nature, and is and should be its <term>imitator</term> <note>original Latin: "Imitator"</note>, he must first well recognize the nature of each and every thing, so that he does not override it, but knows how to follow it in all its <term>limits</term> <note>original Latin: "Limitibus"; the natural boundaries or laws of a substance</note>. Herein it is required that he be a good, well-practiced, and experienced <term>philosopher</term> <note>original Latin: "Philosophus"; in this context, a student of natural science and divine laws</note> of a subtle understanding, so that he may well understand, weigh, and recognize the <term>causes</term> <note>original Latin: "causas"</note> of all things; he should have experienced so much in <term>philosophy</term> that he has brought all its <term>subjects</term> <note>original Latin: "subiecta"; the materials or matters being studied</note> into sufficient knowledge, knows their <term>seeds</term> <note>original Latin: "Semina"</note>, beginning, and element from which they arose, how they are generated, and what they may suffer or undergo in Nature. He should know the power of heat and fire, understand the birthing warmth, and know how all these perform their <term>effects</term> <note>original Latin: "Effectus"</note> in the air, water, and earth. The changes of the seasons should be known to him, as well as how the upper things <note>the celestial bodies/heavens</note> influence and flow into the lower things, and the like.

Therefore, let him <term>conjoin</term> <note>original Latin: "coniungiere"; to join or unite</note> and unite <term>philosophy</term> with <term>alchemy</term>, which is the practice of <term>philosophy</term>; for whoever wishes to come to practice without philosophy is just as if he wanted to fly and had no feathers, or walks without any understanding, like the donkey to its fodder, who does not know why he stretches out his mouth.

Now, if the true <term>philosopher</term> will thus arrange, establish, and consider his <term>practical operations</term> <note>original Latin: "Operationes Practica"</note> and <term>way of working</term> <note>original Latin: "Modum operandi"</note> according to true <term>physics</term> <note>original Latin: "Physica"; the study of the physical/natural world</note>, then the use of these writings and books will be more furthering and helpful to him than can be told in brief; he will also find the benefit in practice and experimentation—like one who receives a rich reward for his labor through the tasting of a lovely dish or food in the mouth. He should also first—which I shall in no way forget to exhort him—call upon and pray to God the Lord, who gives richly to everyone, for grace and understanding, that He might wish to kindle the fire of His Divine grace in the work.

With this, I wish to have directed the favorable reader first to the fear of God, and thereafter to <term>philosophy</term>, but not to <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: "Sophisterey"; deceptive or fallacious reasoning, often contrasted with true natural wisdom</note>; so that before he undertakes to labor at anything, he may pick out the kernel of truth and the foundation of these and other similar writings from the shells, husks, or outermost bark of obscurity; thereafter, as he

# Preface to the Reader.

that which Nature promises, and wishes to seek and find it in the work itself, he should spare no expense to equip himself with all kinds of <term>mechanical instruments</term> <note>original Latin: "Mechanicis Instrumentis"; here meaning the specialized tools of the laboratory</note> that serve the craft. In these, he should also be fairly well-instructed in all manner of manual labor. He must have a well-equipped <term>laboratory</term> <note>original Latin: "Laboratorium"</note> with all kinds of furnaces, glassware, and other supplies, so that if something is needed in haste, it is immediately at hand, and one is not hindered, led astray, or delayed in the middle of the work for lack of tools. Therefore, if he wishes to undertake or begin anything, he must first be well-advised as to everything that belongs to it and what is necessary. He must also have previously learned all the manual techniques of <term>distilling</term>, <term>sublimating</term>, <term>calcining</term>, <term>reverberating</term>, <term>putrefying</term>, <term>casting</term>, and <term>refining</term> <note>original: "distillieren / supplimieren / calcinieren / reuerberieren / putrificieren / giessen / abtreiben"; these are the fundamental chemical processes of the era</note>, etc.

Now, if he has all this, and can, knows, and understands what belongs thereto, then the most important thing is that he does not shy away from any expense, effort, or labor; rather, let him be diligent, industrious, watchful, zealous, and of tireless constancy in his work. He must try things in various ways and repeat them often if they do not immediately succeed according to his wishes. For upon this point of constancy and perseverance in the work, everything depends. The secrets of nature are not opened to the lazy, sleepy, and negligent; for in this matter, one should well consider the saying of the philosopher <term>Epicharmus</term> <note>original Latin: "Epicarmi Philosophi"; a Greek poet and philosopher known for his moral maxims</note>, where he says: "The gods offer their gifts for sale, not for money, but for labor and service."

If the kind reader uses these writings in the manner described, he will not regret the effort and the expense incurred (if he desires to be a true and perfect <term>physician</term> <note>original Latin: "Medicus"</note>). Not only will he recover the value of what he has invested <term>with interest</term> <note>original Latin: "cum foenore"</note> through the noble medicines, but he will also see other things that will delight and please him many times over. It will so enlighten his understanding that he will not be able to wonder enough at the knowledge of nature. He will recognize God more and better, praising, honoring, and glorifying Him in His creatures, helping his neighbor with medicine, and thereby earning for himself both temporal and eternal reward. Thus, he will usefully spend his time in the fear and honor of God and will know how to be sufficiently grateful to God.

May the kind reader, therefore, take this fifth and last part—as well as the first mentioned writings of **Theophrastus Paracelsus** and other philosophers—under his care, and in time, with patience, expect something better, more intelligible, and more detailed. And with this, be commended to Divine protection. Done on the 30th of August, in the year 1604.

## On the Revelation of the Philosophical Materials and Things /
### From which the Mastery is accomplished / in the operation of the Noble and Blessed Stone of the Philosophers.

## Chapter One.

Seven children <note>Often referring to the "Children of the Art," or the seven planetary metals (Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead).</note> and lovers of wisdom, you should diligently mark and observe in this noble art of Nature. The roots and the very best herbs of the philosophers <note>In alchemical "Deckname" (cover-names), "herbs" and "roots" rarely refer to literal plants, but rather to the minerals or metallic "seeds" from which the Stone grows.</note> are in part green mixed with white, in part citrine-colored <note>original: "Citrinfarb"; a lemon-yellow color signaling a specific stage of maturation in the alchemical process.</note> mixed with red and white colors; there are also some of blue colors. The smell and taste of them all is so noble and sweet that nothing sweeter may be found in this world, and the juice that is drawn from them is of such varied colors that it becomes red in the sunshine and white in the moonlight. And these herbs are common, and a heavenly gift, which are found at all times; the ancient philosophers have shrouded and hidden their power and virtue, and wished to write nothing of them nor reveal them, but rather spared no diligence to preserve and hide them most carefully. I, however, have named them to you quite perfectly by their right name, and swear by the Creator of Heaven and Earth that the art is accomplished from these and no other things in this world.
