But before the first year was even out, I had already spent everything I was meant to use for two years and sent it away in smoke.

During this time my *tutor* was severely ill with a hot fever, which in my opinion he caught from the coal fire that we kept burning intensely, just like those in the *Arsenal* at *Venice* get from casting cannons. But when he took a cold drink in such heat, he thereafter passed away; I felt heartfelt sorrow over this, partly because my parents would no longer send me any money—only as much as I needed for my own person. However, so that I might now bring my intended work to an end, I was forced to move home so that I could settle with my guardians and be of my own mind, and also apply my paternal inheritance just as it well pleased me. After I had gathered it all in *Amsterdam* <note>original: "Arendam"</note>, it was worth about 400 crowns. Afterward, I tried a recipe that had been granted to me by an Italian; I kept this man with me until I saw the outcome of this work, for he swore highly that he had experienced it in practice. For this, we bought 2 ounces of gold and 1 ounce of silver; these we first dissolved in a water, then we calcined it for three months before we prepared this powder to perform the projection <note>original: "tingieren," meaning to "tinge" or tint, a common term for the final step of transmutation</note>, which we did according to the contents of the recipe. But it was in vain, and thus our increase became a decrease, and out of 8 ounces only three ounces remained for us—I will say nothing here of other expenses—so that my 400 crowns became 230 crowns. Of that, I gave my Italian 20 crowns so that he could travel to the man from whom he had the recipe, who was said to live in *Milan*, to receive a better report from him; and so I waited the whole winter for

...for him; but I would have had to wait until the Day of Judgment, and so I saw him no more from then on.

But when the joyful summer arrived—though accompanied by a plague <note>original: "Peſtilenz"; the narrator is likely referring to one of the periodic outbreaks of bubonic plague in 16th-century France</note>—I was forced to depart with my other companions for half a year. During that time, I came across an old man who was commonly called "the Philosopher." I joined him and shared my recipes with him, asking him to point out the most prominent ones among them. He showed me ten or twelve that seemed the best to him. After the plague came to an end, I returned to my old place and immediately began to test those same recipes. I worked through the entire winter until **St. John’s Day** <note>June 24th, a common quarterly marker in the legal and liturgical calendar</note>, but I gained just as much from them as I had from the previous ones. My 400 crowns had diminished until I had only 70 left; however, I was not yet despondent. At that time, there was an Abbot who had a recipe that had been written to him from **Rome**, from the court of **Cardinal Armagnac** <note>Georges d'Armagnac (1501–1585), a powerful French cardinal and diplomat known for his interest in the arts and sciences</note>. I joined him, and we each put in 100 crowns, intending to work from a common fund.

After we had built new furnaces of a strange shape, we also had to have an *aqua vitae* <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; literally "water of life," a highly rectified alcohol used as a solvent</note> with which to dissolve an ounce or an ounce and a half of gold. We therefore bought a barrel of good strong wine, from which we produced a great quantity of that same rectified water using a **Pelican** <note>an alchemical vessel used for circulatory distillation, named for its shape which resembles a pelican pecking its own breast</note>; we put it into many glass vessels that we bought for that purpose. After that, we took better gold and calcined it <note>reduced it to powder through heat</note> beforehand for one month. We took one ounce of gold and four ounces of the water and put them into two thick, strong, glazed **retorts** <note>glass bulbs with long, downward-pointing necks used for distillation</note> where one fitted into the other, well-sealed. We placed them in two large round furnaces, for which we bought thirty guilders' worth of coal at once to maintain the fire. This lasted for a whole year, although we also tested other recipes on the side, from which we drew no more profit than from the "Great Work" itself. Namely, we had nothing from either except that we had to keep our fire burning for an eternal time until we might see—as this recipe claimed—the **Coagulation** <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid</note> without a preceding **Solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>.

However, we were not working with the right material, nor was this the true water that was supposed to dissolve our gold. Thus, we found the gold or powder still whole, only a little more subtle. We threw this onto living **mercury** <note>original symbol: ☿</note> according to the instructions of the recipe, but in vain. This vexed us greatly, especially the Abbot, who had boasted loudly before his monks. He was waiting only for the end, at which point he intended to turn the "Lead Well" <note>likely a reference to a specific fountain or a metaphorical source of base metal</note> into gold; but for now, he had to save that for another time. He did this to provide support to the German artist who was traveling past at the time I was in **Paris**. But the Abbot took heart again and advised me that I, for my part, should scrape together three or four hundred crowns...

# Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...whatever I put in, the Abbot also wanted to contribute an equal amount. I was then to travel with him to **Paris**, where there is a great number of <term>laborants</term> <note>original: "Laboranten"; people who work in a laboratory, specifically alchemical practitioners</note>. I was to stay among them for as long as it took until I finally obtained a perfect and true result, which we would then divide as brothers.

Once the pact was made, I again drew funds from my paternal inheritance. When I arrived in **Paris**, I brought 800 crowns with me, intending not to leave until the money was spent or I had found something. I departed from my relatives with no small amount of resentment on their part; they had wanted to make a councilman out of me, believing I was an excellent legal scholar. But I resisted their plans and acted as if I intended to buy a government office with this money. After taking my leave, I set out and reached **Paris** on the third day after **Epiphany** <note>original: "Heiligen drey König tag"; January 6th</note>. I stayed there for a whole month without anyone knowing me. Soon after, I began to visit the craftsmen, goldsmiths, furnace-makers, and others, making such friends that within a month, a hundred <term>artists</term> <note>original: "Artiſten"; in this period, the term referred to practitioners of the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy</note> knew me. 

Some worked on <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: "Tincturen"; substances capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note> of metals through <term>projections</term> <note>original: "Proiectiones"; the act of casting an alchemical powder onto molten metal to trigger transformation</note>, some through <term>cementations</term> <note>original: "Cementationes"; a process of heating metals with powdered chemicals to purify them</note>, others through dissolution, and the majority through the union of the essence of the stone <term>Simrilli</term> <note>a cryptic name for a specific alchemical substance or "stone"</note>. Some engaged in long-lasting boilings, some in the extraction of <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> from metals, and some in the stabilization <note>original: "beſtendigmachung"; also known as "fixation," turning a volatile substance like mercury into a solid that can withstand fire</note> of the same. We were constantly together, now in houses, then in the Cathedral <note>likely referring to Notre Dame de Paris, a common meeting place for alchemists due to its symbolic carvings</note>, for we paid no heed to Sundays or workdays. 

Some said: "Oh, would to **GOD** that we could start our work again, then we would do it right!" Others said: "If only our vessel had remained whole, it would have turned out well." Another said: "If we had had a copper vessel that was perfectly round, we could have stabilized <term>mercury</term> with <term>silver</term> <note>original: "Mercurium mit Luna"; Luna is the alchemical name for silver, associated with the Moon</note>." There was not one of them who did not have an excuse. I turned a deaf ear to them for a long time, for I regretted my expenses, into which I had so carelessly allowed myself to be talked. 

Then there was a powerful and learned **Greek** who came to someone well known to me and promised him great things from the stabilization of <term>mercury from cinnabar</term> <note>original: "Mercurij Cinabris"; cinnabar is the bright red ore from which mercury is extracted</note>. This gave me cause—together with my good friends and for my own part—to prepare the money to accomplish this. For this purpose, we had to have three ounces of fine, thinly beaten silver, from which he formed nails with specially made pliers. These he mixed in and cooked in a furnace for a time. Finally, having dried them well, there were no more than three ounces of silver left—and a little more, which he said was his own. The silver we had previously added had vanished into smoke. But **GOD** knows what benefit we had from this work, since I personally contributed 30 crowns and more to it.

# Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

This rumor of the nails spread through the entire city of **Paris**, so that almost everyone was talking about it, especially those who busied themselves with <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: "Sophiſterey"; in alchemy, this referred to the use of deceptive methods to produce alloys that looked like gold or silver but were not genuine</note>. Just as before, there had been a rumor about copper stoves used for <term>fixing mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium... figieren"; the process of turning liquid mercury into a solid, stable metal</note> into silver. Eventually, a nobleman came to us who was well-learned in all manner of sophistry—indeed, so highly skilled that he could actually earn something from it. He offered his products to the goldsmiths for sale. I struck up a friendship with him, though not without great expense, so that he would not think me poor. I associated with him for an entire year before he explained even the smallest thing to me. At last, he shared his secret with me; however, though he held it in high regard, it was actually worth nothing. Nevertheless, I wrote everything that had happened to my Abbot and sent him the second part of the Work, along with the <term>practical instructions</term> <note>original: "Practica"</note> of the aforementioned nobleman. Upon this, the Abbot wrote back to me that I should remain in **Paris** and spare no expense, especially since I had obtained such a magnificent <term>secret</term> <note>original: "arcanum"; a hidden alchemical recipe or elixir</note>. However, I had resolved in my own mind not to use any material that did not remain stable in the state in which it first appeared. I determined to work on nothing that served roguery or intended to make one rich through the harm of other people. Thus, according to his letter, I stayed there for another year—making three years in total—and went now to this person, then to that one, and especially to those who were rumored to possess something. This rumor of the nails <note>Refers to a common alchemical trick where a nail—usually half iron and half gold—was dipped into a liquid to "prove" transmutation had occurred.</note> spread through the entire city of **Paris**, so that almost everyone knew how to speak of it, especially those who dealt in **sophistry** <note>In this context, "sophistry" refers to "false alchemy": the use of chemical tricks, alloys, or gilding to mimic precious metals rather than achieving true transmutation.</note>, just as there had previously been a rumor about the copper vessel <note>original: "Küpfferin Deſelin"; likely referring to a specific apparatus or a person named Deselin or Desalius</note> for fixing **mercury** into **silver**. I resolved to perform no work that serves for roguery, or to become rich through the harm of other people. So, according to his letter, I stayed there another year, in addition to the two previous years, and went now to this person, then to that one, and especially to those who had a reputation for possessing some knowledge.

### On the Natural Philosophy of Metals ###

...so that I might obtain a firm and steady conviction. While I stood in such doubt, I thought it best to visit experienced **artists** <note>In this context, "artists" refers to practicing alchemists or metallurgists.</note> regarding this matter, setting aside the **deceivers**—of whom I knew well there were many in the land, leading others astray with them. But this doubt increased more and more the longer I considered the manifold ways of working among them. For where there was one who worked only in **Gold** <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol)</note>, there was another who attempted it in **Silver** <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna)</note> and **Copper** <note>original symbol: ♀ (Venus)</note>; some worked with **Lead** <note>original symbol: ♄ (Saturn)</note>, which they called **Sonam** because it passed through the retort along with the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"; quicksilver.</note>. ->While one worked in the **alembic** <note>A distillation apparatus.</note>, there was another, by contrast, who wanted to drive **Lead into Silver and Gold** in glass vials and copper vessels.<-

M." for Balneum Mariae, a gentle heating method using hot water.</note>, so that such diversity, along with the long-windedness of the books, nearly brought me to the point of utter despair. Thus, I read with greater diligence than I had ever done before: first the writings of **Raymundus Lulius**, especially in the **Testament** and the **Codicil** <note>original: "Testamento und Codicillo"; two of the most influential alchemical texts attributed to Llull.</note>, which closely match an **Epistle** he wrote to **King Robert** shortly before his end. I especially compared these against a manuscript that the aforementioned Doctor had given me, finding that his was of no use to him. Thus I resolved within myself to find a single path—contrary to all the aforementioned works I had ever seen—that would harmonize with all the books. I also compared this against the writing of the **Clarification** by **Arnold of Villanova** <note>original: "örterung Arnoldi de villa Noua"; Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, which he placed at the end of his **Great Rosary** <note>original: "grossen Reharij", likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*.</note>. I remained fixed in this opinion and did nothing else but study day and night in my **Resolution** until my manifold senses were ready to attempt such a thing in practice.

First, I built a furnace and thus began to work on the day after Easter—not without many hindrances, which I will not mention here, save only for the reproaches of my friends and neighbors. Some said, "Listen, what is your intention? Have you not wasted enough on this folly?" I also learned on the way that the **Doctor** had died. Therefore, I went to a place known to one of my friends; there I waited for him. I had given this friend orders to sell all my belongings at home, to pay my debtors in part from the proceeds, and to distribute the rest secretly to my friends and also to poor people, so that my friends and others might also share in the gift that God had given me. Most people, however, thought I had fallen into great doubt and adversity because of my undertaken work, and that because of great debts and shame I had to sell everything so that I might move away and perhaps remain entirely unknown, hidden in a foreign land; just as my friend, on the first day of July...

...came to me and recounted [what had happened]; after that, we traveled to **Lausanne** located in **Savoy**, so that from there we might move to a well-known town in Germany, yet with only a few companions so that no one would recognize us—specifically those who had read my little book during my lifetime, which I wrote for the purpose of leading those wandering in **sophistry** <term>In alchemy, "sophistry" refers to false, deceptive, or purely chemical practices that mimic true transmutation but fail to produce the Philosopher's Stone.</term> back onto the right path.

To conclude this first part of mine, I wish to remind everyone of what the **poet** <note>likely referring to a classical author or the common Latin proverb "Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum."</note> sang: *blessed is he who becomes wise through another’s misfortune.* <note>original: "ſeelig iſt der/ der an eines anderen ſchaden witzig wirdt"</note> Let every man take me as an example, learn from my errors, and guard himself against unnecessary expense and avoid the detours that occur in sophistry. To whomsoever it is granted, it is given; it is hidden from the godless, but revealed to the pious. Let everyone understand this: let it be used only for God’s honor and praise. Amen.

**Aristotle**, in the **first book of his Physics**, <note>original: "Ariſtoteles Libro primo Phyſicor."</note> speaking against those who deny first principles, says that one should not dispute with them, but rather with those who acknowledge and admit such principles, yet are blinded by ignorance and do not see the **snake that lies hidden under this grass** <note>original: "der Schlangen/ ſo unter dieſem Kraut verborgen ligt"; a reference to the Latin phrase "latet anguis in herba," meaning a hidden danger or deception.</note> because of the masks they wear; they cannot recognize or distinguish the false from the true which is right before their eyes. I am inclined to write this little book of mine only for the pious and kind-hearted, so that they may receive no small benefit from it.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the author's personal narrative into a formal theoretical treatise on alchemy. The previous page ended with a discussion on how the art is a gift from God rather than a result of mere study.</meta>

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...which is why it is also called Divine, [dealing] with the most principal works; therein shall be explained the errors of the artists of this time, and finally, it will be shown how nature works within the earth in the generation of metals, which the artists on earth must imitate; thereafter, we also wish to indicate the proper and appropriate **Matter** <term>The *Materia Prima* or "First Matter," the foundational substance required to begin the alchemical Work.</term>. Finally, we shall reconcile the most principal points and **terms** <note>original: "Terminos"</note> primarily used in this art, as well as the contradictory sayings of the ancients, for the benefit of the **children of wisdom** <note>A traditional term for initiated alchemists who seek spiritual and physical transformation.</note> and to the shame and detriment of the unwise, all through the authority of the oldest and most learned philosophers.

However, so that we may better explain those who first discovered our art and were its beginners, it is first necessary to cite the teaching of **Saint James** here, which reads as follows:

> Every good and perfect gift is from above, from the Father of Lights. <note>A reference to James 1:17, emphasizing that alchemical success is a divine grace.</note>

This teaching aligns very well with our purpose, especially since our art is so divine, indeed supernatural (in its second operation) as it has always been and still is. It is impossible for man to understand it, neither through reading nor studying—even if they were the wisest and most learned—unless God first reveals it to them. For in this matter, all natural reason and cause are lacking; therefore, it is not unfairly written by some that it is reserved by God only for His own—those who fear, honor, and love Him—as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy (Hermeticism) is attributed.</note>, the great prophet, says:

> I can give thanks to none but God for this discovery.

**Aluidius** <note>An authority often cited in medieval alchemical texts, sometimes associated with Arab philosophers.</note> proves this with these words:

> Know that God has reserved this for the descendants of Adam, and especially for the poor.

This is also proven by **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan; in this context, likely "Pseudo-Geber," the influential 13th-century author of the *Summa Perfectionis*.</note> in his *Summa*, saying:

> Our art and science is kept in the power of God, who gives it to whom He wills.

Therefore, it does not lie in the power of men, nor was it devised or invented by them. But as much as it is natural—and yet followed nature in its first beginnings—many opinions exist in the testimonies regarding its inventors.

There is a great difference between **ripening the unripe** <note>The author views base metals not as different species, but as "unripe" versions of gold.</note> and thereafter birthing something new out of a thing. namely Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. Among these, two contain the other two within themselves: Earth contains Fire, and Water contains Air. As Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval alchemy and logic.</note> says in his *Codicillus* <note>Latin: "Little Manuscript" or "Supplement."</note>: viewed in this way, he speaks of the nature and property of the Oil, which the sophists call Air because it is said to possess more of that nature; but you will not be able to recognize or distinguish this with your eyes. From this it clearly appears that four elements are in our Work, though they are not visible as the majority falsely believe, as will be said hereafter when we define the terms.

It is also called natural because, in its first action, it follows Nature as much as possible, though not in all things, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry," whose Latinized works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says in his *Summa*. But hereupon the works of the ancient philosophers who were before us can be more than sufficiently confirmed for us. These [philosophers], having recognized through their diligent research (as Raymond says in his epistle to King Robert <note>original: "Albertum," likely an error for King Robert of Naples, a traditional recipient of Lullian works</note>, and Albertus Magnus in the book *On Simple Minerals* <note>original: "de simplicibus mineralibus"</note>), that Nature, for the generation of metals, works alone beneath the earth through tedious and constant boiling <note>Alchemical "cooking" or "digestion" refers to the application of steady, low heat over long periods.</note>, to separate the pure from the impure, the perfect from the imperfect, by constant evaporation. This is caused partly by means of the mineral heat, and partly through the warmth of the Sun, which by itself does not cause full ripening—as Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist who spent decades seeking the Stone.</note> explains and as daily experience also indicates and teaches us. For we see clearly in the mines the differences between metals: some are coarser, others more subtle and pure.

Likewise, Rhazes <note>Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, a Persian polymath</note> says in the <term>Book of Lights</term> <note>original: "lib. Luminum"</note>: "If you do not recognize the true dissolution of our body, you labor in vain; for whoever does not know this, everything else will be of no use." This is the Stone of which Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> speaks in his fourth book, when he says:

> Protect me and I will help you; give me what is mine, and I will come to your aid.

He also speaks of the hidden body in his first book:

> The falcon on the peak of the mountain cries out: I am black, white, yellow, citron-red. <note>These colors represent the essential stages of the alchemical transformation: nigredo (blackness), albedo (whiteness), citrinitas (yellowness), and rubedo (redness).</note>

The reason our science is nothing without this union is this: at the time of the "birth" of our Divine Work, the volatile part carries the fixed part away with it. It can be made to remain in the fire and become stable through no other way than through this wondrous and more-than-supernatural <term>Conjunction</term> <note>The sacred marriage or union of opposites in alchemy</note>. According to the inquiries of all philosophers, they say primarily that the stable must become volatile, and the volatile must become stable. This <term>Conjunction</term> must happen precisely at the hour of its birth, as Hali <note>likely Haly Abenragel, an Arab astrologer</note> says in the *Book of Secrets*: "He who does not find our Stone at the time of its birth need not wait for another in its place." For whoever begins our Divine Work without knowledge of the specific hour of its birth will receive nothing from it but useless and vain labor—indeed, the punishment for his error. Rhazes, in the *Book of Commandments*, specifically calls this <term>Conjunction</term> the "Weight of the Sages," and their Rule <note>original: "Regiment"</note> advises everyone to abstain from this Divine Work if they do not know the "Weights" most precisely; the philosophers have hidden this above all things, as can be seen well enough from their many writings.

Therefore, where there is one who confesses that this union occurs on the 7th day, you will soon find another who says it is completed in 40 days; another says in 9 months or in 7 (such as Rhazes); and another at the end of the year, such as Rosinus <note>a common Latin corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note>.

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals. 747

...tery <note>original: "geheimnuß," completing the word from the previous page</note>, you will find barely two who agree on this, even though it is no more than a single term, one day, indeed even one single hour, in which the union is meant to occur through its own <term>cooking</term> <note>original: "Kochung," referring to the alchemical process of decoction or heating</note>.

However, because they have spoken and vowed not to reveal this secret openly to any human, they take pains to describe so many different *terms* <note>original: "Terminos"</note> that they understand among themselves to mean one single thing. Indeed, whoever knows and understands this one thing will find that everything else is nothing but "women's work" and "children's play," as *Socrates* says: "Look, I have shown you the true way of white *Saturn*" (that is, the true preparation of our material, which at first appears like *Saturn* <note>lead</note> and afterwards becomes white through our steady cooking). "If you understand this sufficiently, the rest is nothing but women's work and children's play."

I wish to show by this that nothing is easier than our Work after the union has taken place, because nothing more is needed then than the steady cooking of the two united materials. In this cooking, the much-desired rest will be granted, as the philosopher says in the *Book of Ethics* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Nicomachean Ethics"</note>, that rest is much more pleasant than labor. That our final cooking occurs with rest and without labor is testified by *Rhazes* <note>Rasis</note> in the *Book of the Three Words*, where he says: that all dissolution, *calcination* <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile components</note>, *sublimation*, whitening, and reddening—and whatever else belongs to it to complete our Divine Work—must occur in the fire without removal from it. This is further testified by *Pythagoras* in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" or "Assembly of the Philosophers"</note>, saying that all procedures <note>original: "Regiment"</note> belonging to our Divine Work and *perfection* are fulfilled through cooking alone. Thus also speaks *Barseus* in the very same book: "All your cooking, *tinting* <term>tincturing</term>, and *calcination* must be fulfilled in this Divine Work through cooking alone."

However, so that the fraudulent artists <note>a common term for "false" alchemists or charlatans</note> do not also claim their work is nothing else but cooking, we wish to present here, alongside these, many other opinions of the philosophers, from which their error may be recognized. *Alphidius* says: "In the generation of our Stone, we have no more than one single material (which they properly call a water), and also one cooking, as it occurs in one fire without removal from the same." This is also testified by King *Solomon*: "In the preparation of our Divine Stone (which he calls our *sulfur*), we need no more than one means." *Lilius* also says: "Our Divine Work occurs in one vessel, and through one means and cooking." *Muhammad* <note>Machomet</note> says: "We have no more than one means with one cooking alone, one vessel, in which we complete our Divine Work, both for whitening and reddening."

**Avicenna** was also of this opinion, who spoke in this way far better than many others: All work necessary for the preparation of our **Divine Stone** occurs in one vessel alone, though it is a twofold one. **Geber** also says that the majority of <term>laborants</term> <note>workers or assistants in an alchemical laboratory</note> at this time work in error—which they themselves admit—as there is none among them who does not have three or four furnaces, some even ten or twelve: one for **calcining** <note>reducing a substance to powder through high heat</note>, another for **distilling**, **subliming** <note>heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>, or **solving** <note>dissolving</note>, along with countless vessels they use. What should I say here, however, regarding their "separation of elements," as they call it? Afterward, I shall indicate the right **Matter** through which the Art works its perfection upon the Earth. Since this is the most noble part of the Art—as **Geber** says at the beginning of his *Summa*, and likewise **Avicenna**—it is commanded that all who would abstain from the practice of this Stone should first recognize the true foundations of matters and minerals. In this, I will follow only the most skillful and prominent authors regarding minerals in explaining the things necessary for our work. ### On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

All philosophers hold the opinion that everything that congeals or hardens due to cold mostly contains moisture in its <term>first matter</term> <note>The "materia prima" or fundamental substance from which all things are thought to originate.</note>, as **Aristotle** says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*. Since liquid metals are hardened by cold, their first matter must necessarily be rich in moisture. But **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher famous for his work on natural science and alchemy.</note>, who described minerals more magnificently than anyone else, says that this moisture of metals is not like other watery moistures, because the latter are turned into smoke <note>evaporated</note>, whereas softened metals do not evaporate away. From this, we must conclude that their moisture is mixed with a substance through which it is preserved in the fire. Now, there is nothing that resists fire except <term>viscous humidity</term> <note>original: "viscosa humiditas"; a sticky, oily moisture that was thought to give metals their flexibility and resistance to heat.</note>, which is mixed with earthly subtlety, as **Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemical writer.</note> says and daily experience teaches. Therefore, it is well believed that the moisture of metals is as described; but experience also teaches us that some parts of the metals vanish into smoke, yet they are not entirely consumed in the fire. Thus, we must admit with all writers of this Art that two kinds of moisture are required for the birth of metals: an external one and an internal one.

The first is a coarse moisture, not sufficiently mixed with its earthiness; therefore, it is easily consumed like smoke by the fire. The latter, however, is entirely subtle and mixed with its earth in the best possible way, so that the two become a single, closely united matter. This moisture cannot be divided or consumed by the fire; rather, both remain together in the fire or leave it at the same time. From this moisture **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury often refers to the philosophical principle of fluidity and volatility, not just the liquid metal.</note> is born, as we see and learn from daily experience. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> testifies to this, saying: "This makes us certain that both materials, as said before, are perfectly united in it; for either the earthiness keeps the moisture with it, or the moisture carries the earthiness away." This was also well recognized by **Albertus**, who investigated the cause of metals most precisely: namely, that Mercury is always mobile and fluid because one part dominates the other. In the other, the moisture (which is the cause of flowing) persists, but the dry earthiness prevents it from sticking to the first. **Albertus’s** opinion is further strengthened by the *Book of Simple Minerals*, where it is written: "The first matter of metals is a viscous humidity <note>original: "viscosa humiditas"</note>, unburnable, and very strongly united in the ores of the earth." This agrees beautifully with **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy.</note>, who says in his *Summa* <note>Referring to the "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," a core text of medieval alchemy.</note> that the right, true matter of metals is a living mercury; for immeasurable nature creates Mercury out of the aforementioned mixed matter. **Bonus of Ferrara** says: "Mercury is the closest matter to the metals, but primarily the viscous humidity with its subtle..."

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...earths mixed together. **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath and legendary father of Islamic alchemy whose works were fundamental to European science.</note> says in the description of Mercury, which he places in his *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "Summa"; specifically Geber’s *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, one of the most influential alchemical textbooks.</note>, that the moisture of Mercury is ordered through the help of its subtle earths in its inward composition.

Therefore, it is necessary for us to diligently consider the work of Nature in the birthing of all things, through which the properties of matter are mixed—which the philosophers have called the **acting principle** <note>original: "das wirckend"; the active force or agent that triggers change in a substance.</note>, because matter cannot make or bring itself forth on its own—that is, it cannot demonstrate its own action. As **Aristotle** speaks, it does not prove its own effect. Therefore, when Nature created Mercury as the "Matter of Salt" <note>This likely refers to the "body" or salt-like stability required for the birth of metals.</note> for the birth of metals, she very wisely added to it its own acting principle: namely, a **fatty mineral earth** of its own kind, entering into the minerals through long-lasting decoction <note>A process of heating or "cooking" within the earth over long periods.</note>, which we commonly call a **Sulfur**. This Sulfur is to be regarded in relation to Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note> as the curdling agent <note>original: "die gegen der Milch"; literally "that which is against milk," referring to rennet used in cheesemaking.</note> is to milk, and as the man is to the woman, and as the active principle is to matter. The philosophers have named two kinds of **Sulfur**: one that is quite easily fluid, and the other quite hard and non-fluid.

In order for Nature to demonstrate such acting power, it might be shown that the salt of the Sulfur within the matter to which it is added causes them, in the composition of some metals, to be hardened in a wondrous way, or on the other hand, to become entirely fluid. But other minerals of inferior composition do not become fluid by the **action of sulfur** <note>original: "actione ſulphuris"</note>, such as the **Marcasites** <note>A common mineral, iron pyrite, often mistaken for gold or silver ore.</note> or **Magnesia**, so that they are not volatile, and others of the same kind. Since the active principle cannot be a **part of the composite** <note>original: "theil des Compoſiti"</note>, as **Aristotle** says, after Nature has mixed the aforementioned Sulfur with Mercury in the mines in a wondrous way, she makes from it the precious metal, namely **Gold**, solely through **perfect decoction**—that is, to separate the Sulfur from it. This is its action, and this is the reason why it is more perfect than all other metals. Since we further see in Nature that it cannot be transformed into anything better, for that reason it also unites and mixes easily with Mercury, because it is nothing other than Mercury cooked with its own Sulfur and finally entirely separated from this decoction. This separation of the Sulfur is the perfection of Gold, whereas in other metals it remains; this is the cause of their imperfection. Hence, **Silver** is more imperfect than Gold, and **Copper** more imperfect than Silver, solely due to a lack of complete maturation, through which alone the active principle—namely, the Sulfur—is separated from it. In this lies the foremost secret of our entire Art.

Since, then, Art must follow Nature, it is necessary that it completes our **Divine Work**, so that the acting principle may be separated from it, which...

We have said above that the perfection or imperfection of metals lies only in whether the **Sulfur**, as the **acting principle** <term>acting principle|In alchemical theory, Sulfur is the active, masculine force that gives form, color, and "ripeness" to the passive, feminine Mercury.</term>, is still with the matter or separated from it. Now, however, it is further to be known that Nature makes use of another way, which, although it appears somewhat contrary to the first, is yet entirely the same if one pays diligent attention to the end toward which Nature's intention is directed. This is nothing other than to purify the metals and separate them from all [excess] Sulfur. For what the Art accomplishes in the first way through perfect **decoction** <note>A term for "cooking" or heating a substance over time to achieve a higher state of purity or maturity; it was believed the earth's internal heat "cooked" base metals into gold over centuries.</note>, Nature achieves through lengthy and constant cooking: namely, to purify the imperfect metals for so long until they finally become the best gold.

Likewise, daily experience teaches us that one often finds **Saturn** <term>Saturn|The alchemical and astrological name for lead, associated with the slow-moving planet and the metal's heavy, "cold" nature.</term> in silver mines, and in some, both mixed together, so that the silver looks as if it were not yet perfect. For this reason, those skilled in mining advised me that we should let it remain longer in the closed veins [of the earth] for thirty or forty years, so that the purest matter does not evaporate, until it is completely and utterly perfected. I have also heard from his miners that such things often occur. Therefore, it follows from this how Nature operates in the stability of metals.

In this way, the Art must follow Nature: namely, to perfect the imperfect through the separation of Sulfur. ...mixed with earth. *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of alchemy.</note> says in the description of *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> which he sets down in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, a highly influential medieval alchemical handbook.</note> that the moisture of *Mercury* is ordered by the help of its subtle earth within its internal composition.

Therefore, it is necessary for us to diligently consider Nature's work in the birth of all things, through which the property of the Matter is mixed, which the Philosophers have called the **acting principle** <term>acting principle|A translation of the Latin *agens*, referring to the active, masculine force (Sulfur) that shapes the passive, feminine matter (Mercury).</term>, since it cannot make or bring itself forth—that is, it cannot show its effect. Therefore, when Nature created **Mercury** as the matter of Salt in the generation of metals, she very wisely added to it the specific acting principle: namely, a fatty mineral earth of its own kind, entering the minerals through long-term cooking, which we commonly call **Sulfur**. In relation to Mercury, this is to be considered as the **rennet to milk** <note>Just as rennet causes milk to solidify into cheese, Sulfur was thought to "fix" or solidify liquid Mercury into solid metal.</note>, and as the man to the woman, and as the active force to the matter. The Philosophers have called it two kinds of **Sulfur**: one entirely volatile and fluid, the other very hard and unyielding. But so that Nature may show such active power, it might demonstrate the Salt of the **Sulfur** in the matter to which it is added; it causes, in a wondrous way, the composition of some metals so that they become hardened, and others so that they become entirely fluid. Since we further see this in Nature, it cannot be transformed into something better; for this reason, it also unites and aligns with **Mercury**, since it is nothing other than **Mercury** cooked with its own **Sulfur**, and finally entirely separated from this cooking. And the separation of the **Sulfur** is the perfection of Gold; however, when it remains in other metals, this is the cause of their imperfection. Hence Silver is also more imperfect than Gold, and Copper more imperfect than Silver, solely due to the lack of full ripening, through which alone the acting principle—namely, the **Sulfur**—is separated from it. In this consists the primary secret of our entire Art.

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...all Philosophers have hidden, and in this case, have pointed toward Nature, whose properties they have also sufficiently indicated.

All other metals were seen as 'imperfect' or 'immature' versions of gold that had not yet reached completion.</term>. As we have said before, the perfection or imperfection of metals lies only in whether the **Sulfur**, as the acting principle, is still with the matter or has been separated from it. We have also sufficiently mentioned the first path which Nature is accustomed to using in the beginning—namely, in the birth of metals, and especially Gold.

Now, however, it is further to be known that Nature makes use of and employs another path which, although it appears somewhat contrary to the first, is yet entirely identical to it if one pays diligent attention to the goal toward which Nature’s intent is directed. This is nothing other than to purify the metal and separate it from all Sulfur. For what the Art achieves in the first path through **perfect cooking**, Nature accomplishes through long-lasting and steady **cooking** <term>cooking|Also called 'coction,' this refers to the natural heat of the earth that slowly matures base metals into gold over decades or centuries.</term>—namely, by purifying the imperfect metals for so long until they finally become the best gold.

Likewise, daily experience teaches us that one often finds **Lead** <term>Lead|original: *Saturnum*. Alchemists used the names of planets to refer to metals; Saturn corresponds to lead.</term> in the **mines** <term>mines|original: *Mineren*, referring to the ore-rich veins within the earth.</term> of silver, and in some, both are mixed together, so that the silver looks as if it were not yet perfect. Therefore, the mining experts advised me that we should let it remain in closed veins for another thirty or forty years, so that the purest matter does not evaporate before it is completely perfected.

The great *Albertus* <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose writings on minerals were foundational to later alchemists.</note> also says that this once happened in the Kingdom of **Liburnia or Slavonia** <note>original: *Liburniæ vel Sclauoniæ*; historical regions in the modern-day Balkans known for their mineral wealth.</note>. I have heard the same from his miners, that such things often occur. Therefore, it follows here how Nature behaves in the stability of metals. In this way, the Art must follow Nature—namely, to perfect the imperfect through the separation of Sulfur. Specifically, when the mentioned Stone is cast upon them while they are fluid, they are quickly purified into the best gold by means of the **excessive cooking** <note>The Philosopher's Stone was believed to possess a concentrated, "over-cooked" heat that could perform in an instant what Nature takes forty years to achieve.</note> which they receive through the addition of our Art. It is no different than the many paths Nature uses in the purification of metals; there are also many paths in that place (I mean in their Perfection). In the same way, we use the same path on Earth for the stabilization of our natural gold, no differently and no more distinctly than the mineral gold, using the very same matter on Earth which Nature herself uses in the mines...

...mines, as Aristotle testifies in the book *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphysicæ"</note>, saying: That from identical agents and matter, identical effects always arise, although what occurs in between may be different, for this [the agent] and the matter are two distinct things. They named it "enlivened Mercury" to distinguish between common mercury and this special Mercury, because common mercury remains as it is since Nature has not mixed its own active agent into it. Therefore, most people falsely believe that common mercury and common sulfur are the true matter of metals; however, it never happens that both are mixed together at the same time in the mines. For this reason, they cannot be the true matter of metals in the mines of the Earth or in our Art on Earth, as **Geber** says in his *Summa* when speaking of the beginning of the Art. And in another place, he says: "Our Mercury is nothing other than a viscous water, perfected with its metallic Sulfur." This is the true matter that Nature prepares for our Art and has established in a certain and true form known to the Philosophers, without any change in itself. Likewise, **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina.</note> also says: "Nature has prepared for us one single matter, which our Art cannot create for itself in the slightest degree." I will prove that this separation is false as previously stated: namely, that two elements are enclosed within the other two, which results in one being unable to recognize their true separation, let alone their perfect union.

We see from experience, however, that their elements, when so separated, have no commonality with the nature of true elements, as *Valerandus* and others say. Take for example their **oil**, which they call **Air**; it moistens everything it touches, which is contrary to the true property of the nature of **Air**. I believe enough has been said regarding the nature and property of the elements and their conversion, which is necessary in this our Art, so that the **Children of Truth** <note>A term used by alchemical authors to address their students and fellow seekers of wisdom.</note> may recognize the fantasy of current erring artists and know to flee from it.

But the **Soul** and everything of its kind they called that which is volatile of itself and has the power to carry the Body away with it and keep it from the Fire; and this they called **volatile** <note>original: *flüchtig*.</note>. The **Spirit**, however, they called that which has the power to hold the Body and Soul together, to unite these two so that they cannot be separated from one another, whether perfectly or imperfectly. Although in our Divine Work nothing new or foreign enters from the beginning (I mean after the first preparation), neither in the middle nor at the end, the Philosophers have, out of various considerations, called this one and the selfsame thing sometimes **Body**, sometimes **Soul**, and sometimes **Spirit**, though enough has been said of this above. 

Firstly, when our Matter is volatile, they call it **Soul**, because it carries the Body with it. Afterward, that which was hidden becomes manifest in our **cooking** <note>The process of "digestion" or applying steady heat to the substance.</note>; then the Body shows its power by means of the Spirit—that is, the Soul remains, to bring the same into its own nature (namely into **Gold**), which is to be **sealed** <note>original: *sigieren*; from the Latin *sigillare*, meaning to seal or fix permanently.</note> with its power through the help of our art. Through our long and steady cooking, this acquires such power that it transforms all metals to which it is added into the best **Gold**, turning them to be exactly like the mineral kind. I have also sufficiently indicated above why it can perfect the imperfect ones.

Because no dissimilar simples <term>simplicia</term> <note>Refers to basic, unmixed substances in their elemental state.</note> can be united in their qualities or be mixed together, so also our **Work**—which consists solely of the blessed **Mercury**—can in no way be mixed with any foreign **Sulphur** that has remained in the metals due to a lack of ripening, as mentioned above. But because it is entirely powerful and perfect, it can separate the aforementioned **Sulphur** from the metals and turn the remaining **Mercury** into **Gold**. As we then see, when one performs a **Projection** <note>The final stage of the Great Work: casting the finished Elixir or Stone upon base metal to transform it.</note> upon common **Mercury**, we find that it is entirely turned to gold. But the opposite is seen when it is cast upon [base] metals: out of one pound, barely 6 ounces remain. Yet the more they are cooked, the less they are purified in that manner.

Now I will bring the second part to an end and turn toward the third part, in which I will explain the true **Practice** <note>original: *Practicam*.</note> amidst many riddles, which God reveals to all His believers and lovers who diligently read through these my writings. May He give them true understanding through His **Holy Spirit** and to the honor and praise of His name, who is blessed in eternity.

# The Third Part of the Booklet by Denis Zachaire the Frenchman,
## Concerning the Practice of the Divine Work.

<note>Denis Zachaire (1510–1556) was a French alchemist whose "Opuscule" (The Little Work) became a classic. The name "Galli" is Latin for "the Frenchman."</note>

The entire world has been written of by the **Philosophers** and through the **Cosmographers**, divided into three primary parts: namely, into **Asia, Africa, and Europe**, under the four directions: Rising, Setting, Midday, and Midnight <note>East, West, South, and North.</note>. Therein rule many Emperors, Kings, Princes, Regents, and Lords, each of whom possesses many and varied things for his pleasure—both for their rarity and for the powers within these things. However, the latter <note>The inner powers</note> are not as readily accepted as the former <note>External luxury</note>, which I have learned through experience. I have traveled through many and various lands, and precisely where there are the most learned people, it is there (though to my own detriment) that the learned are quite poor and despised; indeed, they are held in no honor. Conversely, the unwise and the rich are held in great value. Where there is a lack of experienced and learned men, in those same places the wise are held in high esteem, and especially by those of the highest rank. 

It is exactly the same with **Metallic Ores** (from which **Gold** and other **Metals** come). In those places where they are not found, they are held in high and dear regard. Likewise, they are despised by the rich who have much of them. But for the despised and lowly, who have no perfection, their eyes are blinded so that they do not recognize the precious and the perfect. 

For this reason, the **Wise** are angered; when they see that fools are preferred over them, they depart elsewhere to demonstrate the power of their wisdom in other places. This was done in ancient times by a **Prince** who set himself to have no rest until he had made the other part of the world—beyond that which he already possessed—subject to him. He sought to do this through the help of his soldiers and especially his faithful **Steward** <note>In alchemical allegory, the Prince often represents the "King" or the primary substance, while the "Steward" represents the chemical agent or "mercury" that facilitates the work.</note>. As he then deliberated with him, he made many and various friendships with foreigners. However, because these foreigners were not very faithful to him, but instead thought they would be better received by other Emperors, they became estranged from him (as is the way of spies) and revealed all his intentions to them. These others, however, made little of it, for they knew that no earthly power could withstand their own—and how much less the undertaking of this Prince. 

Meanwhile, we see that at court and in the houses of Princes, nothing is practiced but gambling, dancing, singing, and the like; precious time is consumed with useless play. Indeed, the ears are offered up to flatterers, whisperers, and fools, but the **Wise** are despised and the **Philosophers** mocked—whom the great potentates and princes of old were once not ashamed of. But in the meantime, the aforementioned Prince, with the help of his soldiers, has captured a prominent city of the Empire; there the Emperor recruited many people, and...

->all power belongs to the Pope, or Emperor, or<-

## Dispute and Conversation
### of Gold and Mercury against the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin><unclear>Point in the middle of the war</unclear></margin>
A true philosopher <term>philosopher: in this context, a practicing alchemist or "lover of wisdom"</term> writes / and swears by God and his soul / declares and says: You lovers of the Art <term>the Art: "The Great Art" of alchemy, or the Hermetic Art</term> / out of true favor and compassion for those who have sought for a long time / that our entire Work springs from only one thing / and is completed within itself / and requires nothing more than dissolution / and its own hardening <note>original: "wider hertung," referring to the alchemical principle of *solve et coagula*—the repeated process of dissolving a solid into liquid and solidifying it again to achieve purity.</note> / and this must happen of its own accord without any foreign things / just as ice in a dry vessel / placed over the fire / is turned to water by the warmth / so it is also with our Stone / and it requires no more help than the artist's manual labor / and the natural fire / for of its own power it could not accomplish this even if it lay in the earth for an eternity / therefore one must help it / but not in such a way / that one adds foreign and contrary things to it / but rather / just as God gives us the grain in the field / and we must thresh, grind, and bake it / so that it becomes bread / so it is here as well.

<margin>Ez</margin>
God has created this ore for us / so that we might take it and, by destroying the coarse body / take out the good that is within / cast away the superfluous / and make a medicine <term>medicine: the alchemical elixir or "Tincture," believed to heal "sick" (base) metals into gold and cure human ailments</term> out of the poison / and so that you may understand this all the better / I will write for you a fine conversation and disputation that occurred between the Philosopher's Stone, Gold, and Mercury / so that those who have sought for a long time / and who know how to work with metals and minerals / may easily arrive at the true foundation / and it will be necessary / that one learns to recognize every thing in the earth well, both inside and out / and what it is capable of in the foundation of nature.

Now, Gold and Mercury once came to our Stone / with armed hand / intending to overcome it / and Gold began in a defiant manner and spoke: O you poisonous worm and dragon <note>The "dragon" or "worm" is a common alchemical symbol for the raw, volatile, or "mercurial" matter that must be "slain" or fixed during the Work.</note> / why do you exalt yourself above me and my brother Mercury / seeing as I am the very best and most constant metal / and all princes and lords / as well as the common man, seek their wealth in me / and in my brother Mercury / whereas you, of all metals...

# A Conversation between Gold and Mercury
## (and the Philosopher's Stone)

[...that you are an] enemy, and you know that all physicians <term>physicians: originally "Medici," referring to doctors of medicine who used gold in tinctures</term> highly praise and laud me for the health of mankind.

->Answer of our Stone.<-

Dear Gold, why do you not rage against God, and ask Him why He did not create that which is in me within you as well?

->Gold.<-

God has given me honor, beauty, and glory, which is why the whole world desires me; because I am also the most stable metal both within and without the fire, I am loved by everyone. But you are volatile <term>volatile: "flüchtig," meaning a substance that evaporates or escapes when heated</term> and unfaithful, and you deceive people; for one sees that whoever works with you, you flee from their hands.

->The Stone.<-

Dear Gold, it is true: God has bestowed upon you honor, beauty, and stability, and for such things you should rightly be grateful to God, and not despise others alongside you. But that you thus diminish me, you do so with untruth. I say that you are not the Gold of which the philosophers <term>philosophers: here meaning alchemical masters like Hermes or Geber</term> write; rather, that very thing is hidden within me. For although it is true that I am volatile in the fire, you know well that I am ordained to this by God and Nature, and my moisture <term>moisture: the "mercurial" or liquid principle necessary for transformation</term> serves the worker's benefit. 

If he can rightly extract it, the permanent soul <note>original: "bestendige Seel," referring to the fixed, non-volatile essence that remains after the "moisture" is removed.</note> remains within me, which is far more stable than you and all your brothers and companions—which no fire nor water may consume nor destroy while the world stands. Thus, I am also not to blame if the seekers cannot work or prepare me correctly, often adding foreign and contrary things like water and powder and the like, thereby ruining my innate nature and properties. 

Furthermore, among a hundred thousand one finds hardly one who works with me; instead, they all seek with you and your brother and companions <note>Referring to common Gold and Mercury (Quicksilver) found in shops.</note>, in which they all fail and work falsely, as one sees in all of them—that they achieve nothing and spend their money uselessly, thereby falling into ruin and poverty. For this, you, Gold, bear the most blame, because you know particularly well that outside of me no true Gold or Silver can be made; rather, I am capable of all things. Why then do you allow the whole world to work only with you and your brother Mercury? If you were sincere and desired to act honestly, you would warn people against harm; therefore, I can rightly say with the truth that you yourself are that very deceiver.

<header>Against the Philosopher’s Stone.</header>

### Gold.

I will prove it through the philosophers <note>original: "Philosophis," referring to the ancient masters of alchemy</note> that the art can be accomplished through me and my brother Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>; for read Hermes <note>original: "Hermetem," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, who writes thus: "The Sun is its Father, and the Moon is its Mother." <note>This is a famous quote from the Emerald Tablet, a foundational alchemical text.</note> For I am compared to the Sun, as the philosophers—many of whom could be cited here—write quite clearly and plainly about it: that the tinctures <term>tinctures: medicinal or transformative substances intended to "dye" or change the nature of a base metal into gold</term> as well as the metals must be composed and put together from Sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> and Mercury. And the Sulfur should be red and incombustible <note>original: "unuerbrennlich"</note>, and stable in the fire; and the Mercury should be clear, pure, and purged. And they write without any digression, calling me openly by name and saying that in me, Gold, is the well-cooked, stable, incombustible red Sulfur, which is then true and obvious to everyone: that I am the better metal and possess the best Sulfur, which cannot be burned in the fire and is entirely fixed <term>fixed: "fix," referring to a substance that remains solid and does not evaporate or change when exposed to high heat</term>.

At this, Mercury also sided with Gold and spoke: It is true what his Lord Brother Gold has recounted, and it can be proven through the aforementioned masters. Furthermore, everyone knows generally what love and unity these two have for each other above all other metals. This alone is plainly visible here: when one wishes to perform gilding <note>The process of applying a thin layer of gold to another surface</note>, one can join and unite Gold and Mercury together; what then might not happen with great effort and labor, more diligence, and a long time of work?

### The Stone.

The Stone spoke with a laughing mouth: Truly, you are both well-deserving of being laughed at for your "proofs." And I wonder, especially at you, Gold—since you boast so highly of yourself in many things and yet have no more understanding. Do you think that the ancient philosophers wrote in their writings so plainly according to common understanding, wanting to be understood exactly according to those very words?

### Gold.

These cited masters have written no untruth, and they agree with one another regarding my virtue. However, there have indeed been others who searched for my cousins and powers in other unbecoming things, such as in various herbs, animals, blood, urine, seeds, sperm <note>original: "Spermaten"</note>, and the like; and those people surely failed and perhaps also wrote falsely. But the aforementioned masters have good testimony that they truly possessed the Art; therefore, their writing is truly to be believed.

# A Dialogue of Gold and Mercury

->The Stone.<-

Do not doubt me in this, for it is all true, that they <note>The "philosophers" or ancient alchemical masters.</note> certainly possessed the Art; yet I except some whom you have cited, for there are a few among them who did not possess it for certain, but rather wrote about it only by hearsay. But where they simply use the names of Sol <note>original: "Solis"; the Sun or Gold</note> and Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>, they do so for the sake of the ignorant and the unworthy, to hide the Art from them; for they well know that such people only focus on the bare letters and names, and on the written recipes and processes, and do not reflect upon the foundation of the matter. 

But the wise and industrious read with understanding and consider well how one thing agrees with another; they draw a foundation from this and thus devise, from the speculation and sayings of the philosophers, the right Matter <note>original: "Matery"</note>, which no philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"</note> has described or indicated by its right name. They prove this themselves when they say: "Where we write most clearly according to common understanding, there we have most hidden the Art. But where we speak in figures, parables, and proverbs, there we have truly brought it to light." 

And where they withhold something regarding gold and mercury, they soon after explain themselves and say that their Gold is not common gold and their Mercury is not common mercury. For gold, by reason of its perfection, can never be further advanced <note>original: "verhindert," here meaning changed or pushed beyond its already perfect state</note>, because it has already become a metal of perfection. Even if one were to extract its colors a thousand times and work with it in a most skillful manner, it can do or color no more than the color it already possesses within itself. Therefore, the philosophers write that one should seek in imperfect things, and thus one will find perfection—just as you may read in the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario," referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note>. Likewise, Lully <note>original: "Lulius," referring to Raymond Lully, a major figure in alchemical literature</note> writes: "That which is to be improved must not be perfect; a perfect thing does not change, it sooner perishes."

->Gold.<-

I know well that they write this, but that may be understood as referring to my brother Mercury; he is still imperfect, and if we both mix with one another, then he is made perfect by me. For there is a Female and Male gender; therefore, the philosophers say the Art is entirely a homogeneous thing <term>homogeneous: original "Homogenium," meaning a substance of a single, uniform nature or kind</term>. You see this clearly in humans: no child can be born without man and woman, but only through the mixing of both. The same is also to be seen in all animals that have life.

## The Stone.

Your brother Mercury is indeed imperfect, but he is not the Mercury of the Sages. Even if you were to mix yourselves together and stand in the fire for many years, it would be impossible for you to be truly united. As soon as Mercury feels the fire, he escapes from you into the heights and sublimates <note>original: "supplimiert"; the process of a substance turning directly from a solid or liquid into a vapor</note> at the top, leaving you lying at the bottom. And if you are joined together with sharp water <note>original: "scharpffem Wasser"; typically referring to nitric acid or other strong mineral acids used to dissolve metals</note>, and are thus dissolved and coagulated, you yield nothing more than a dead powder and precipitate. If one then throws this upon imperfect metals, it does not tincture <note>original: "tingiert"; in alchemy, the power of the Stone to "stain" or transform a base metal into gold</note> them; instead, one finds only your original gold again—exactly as much gold as was added at the beginning—and your brother Mercury escapes from you entirely.

The seekers of the art of Alchemy have experienced this sufficiently for many years now and have learned it to their own detriment. But when you cite the saying of the ancients—that the Art is entirely a homogeneous substance <term>original: "Homogenium"; a substance of the same nature or kind throughout</term>, and that no child is born without a man and a woman—and you think the philosophers intend to examine you and your brother Mercury, that is worth nothing. It is poorly and incorrectly understood by you, even if they wrote it correctly and well. I tell you in truth that this is the very cornerstone that the ancients laid, upon which many thousands have stumbled and gone astray.

Do you think that metals must behave exactly like other things that have life? This is what happens with all false workers of the Art: when you read such things in the books of the philosophers, you do not fundamentally reflect on whether it agrees with what comes before or after. For what the ancient and true philosophers described regarding the Art with such figurative words is understood by me alone, and by no other thing in the world. That alone is the truth, and without it, no righteous and true gold or silver can be made.

## Gold.

God forbid! Do you not fear sin, and are you not ashamed of lies, that you are so immeasurable? How dare you claim for yourself alone everything that so many wise and learned people have written about this Art for many hundreds of years? After all, you are but an unripened, coarse poison and an unclean thing. You yourself confess that the Art is a homogeneous substance of one nature, yet you further claim that outside of yourself no true gold or silver can be made, even though it is well known that many have sought it so diligently and industriously through other ways, such as Particulars <term>original: "Particularien"; chemical processes intended to produce small amounts of gold or transform only a portion of a metal, rather than a total transformation</term>...

Gold responds by accusing the Stone of arrogance and being a "coarse poison," defending the long history of alchemical study and "Particular" works.</summary>

### The Stone.

O dear Gold, do not wonder so much that I have told you such things, and do not call me a liar so boldly and shamelessly, for I am older than you; and even if I had erred in this matter, you ought rightly to spare my age, for you well know that one should honor the aged.

But so that I may prove that I have spoken the truth, to the rescue of my honor, I will do so through your own cited masters, whom you surely cannot reject.

Firstly, Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism and alchemy</note> writes—truly and without lies, but certain and most true—that what is below is like what is above, and what is above is like what is below, so that one may attain the miracles and wonder-signs of a single thing <note>This is a direct translation of the opening of the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Western alchemy</note>.

So also writes Aristotle <note>Medieval alchemists often attributed chemical texts to the Greek philosopher Aristotle to grant them authority</note>: "How wonderful a thing this is, for it has everything within it that we require; it kills itself, and receives life back from itself; it marries itself, it impregnates itself, and gives birth from itself. It dissolves itself in its own blood, and hardens itself again with the same, and becomes White and Red <note>The "White" and "Red" stages (Albedo and Rubedo) are the final steps in creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> of its own accord; and we do nothing further to it, nor do we change anything, except that we separate the earthiness and coarseness from it."

Plato speaks of me thus: It is just one, and the same thing in itself; it has a body, a soul, a spirit, and the four elements over which it rules, and it has no need to borrow anything from other bodies, for it gives birth to itself; from it alone, and in it, are all things. I could present many more such testimonies, but because it is not necessary, I will omit them for the sake of brevity.

But since you mention the "particulars" <term>particulars; localized alchemical processes that only partially transform metals or work with specific substances, rather than the "Universal" work of the Great Stone</term>, the situation is as follows: There are some who have gone so far with me that they were able to extract my tincturing <note>original: "tingierenden"; the power to "stain" or transform a base metal into gold</note> spirit and mix it with other metals and minerals. Through much labor, they brought it so far that I gave off a little of my virtues and powers to the metals that were somewhat related to me. However, this succeeded for very few, and some discovered it only by chance; and because they did not recognize the source from which the tincture comes, they could proceed no further, and yet there is no great use in it.

But if the artist had looked further for my own wife, and united me with her, I could have tinctured a thousand times more; instead, they have always [spoiled] <meta>catchword: "vers-" likely "verstellt" (distorted) or "verstört" (ruined)</meta> my nature with foreign things...

Therefore the ancients write: "Our gold is not visible, and our <term>Mercury</term> cannot be obtained except from the softened bodies." Therefore, out of one thing—which is called the Water of the Spirit and the Body—a medicine is made. Hence it is said that this "man" and these riddles deceive many fools. The Art requires only one thing, which is well known to everyone; and many other things are desired in place of this, and yet no single thing is to be compared to it. It is indeed humble and quite subtle, but one should not despise it, for it produces and completes marvelous things. After that, strengthen your reason and sharpen your senses, and read with understanding, for it must have its natural time, like the fruit on the tree or like a grape on the vine; and be of good will and intention, otherwise God will not give it to you; for GOD gives it to those who desire to do good with it, and takes it from those who intend to undertake evil with it. May GOD give his blessing and understanding,

# Follow several
## Korndorffer’s Particulars. <note>In alchemy, "Particularia" refers to specific recipes or processes intended to work on individual metals or achieve specific results, rather than the "Universal" work of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

### To make a water that dissolves gold.

## Following is the Highest Art of Purification.

Likewise, take 2 Loth of fine silver without gold / and 3 Loth of <term>Bismuth</term> <note>original: "Wißmat."</note> / drive them into one another on the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "Test"; a shallow, porous dish used in assaying.</note> until the <term>brightening</term> <note>original: "Blick"; the sudden flash of light that occurs when the silver becomes pure during cupellation.</note> / 28 times / then the silver with its luster will collapse together and rise / into the highest *sphere of the Sun* <note>The "sphere of the Sun" represents gold; the author claims this process makes the silver take on the properties of gold.</note> / when you have accomplished the work / then take the silver with 5 times as much weight of Mercury as it comes from the mine / make it into pieces / and place it *layer upon layer* <note>original: "stratum super stratum."</note> in a pointed flask; let it flow strongly in the <term>wind furnace</term> <note>A furnace that uses a natural or forced draft of air to reach very high temperatures.</note> / and after half an hour a <term>Regulus</term> <note>original: "König"; a button of purified metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible.</note> will settle / refine this by itself / and you will have *gold elevated in color, that is, Colored* <note>original: "Gold elevatum colore, id est, Coloratum."</note> / do this a second time / and tested on the cupel with its old Lead / whatever remains there / is preserved in all tests / do not cease until you have infused the highest degrees into it / through the art of my revelation.

There are two secret *Saturns* <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead.</note> through which silver may come to great worth / the first is the old Saturnal Lead / the <term>Regulus of Antimony</term> / the other perfect Lead is not called Saturnal / but rather Astralic / yet they both have / a wonderful similarity in one another for purifying other metals.

Take a cast Regulus of Antimony by itself, 2 Loth / less half a Quintin / and two Loth of fine silver / let them be driven into one another / on a brick cupel until it fumes away / thereafter take as much again and do the same / do this eight times / thereafter take one Loth of common Lead / and three Loth of Bismuth / and drive it until it all disappears / do this always with as much Lead / and apply Bismuth 20 times / thus the silver is highly purged / place it in the <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "brennent Wasser"; usually referring to strong acid or aqua fortis.</note> / and it will dissolve / after the Lead, the <term>Aqua Fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid.</note> no longer remains.
